Contents

Deep reinforcement learning, from the loop to turbulence control

Seven lessons that build one idea at a time, each led by pictures: the learning loop, values, policy gradients, actor–critic on PDEs, the algorithm families and Gymnasium, surrogates for an airfoil, and multi-agent control of turbulence. Pick a lesson, or jump straight to a section.

I wrote this guide while working through the projects on this site, to have one place where every idea of deep reinforcement learning for fluid mechanics is drawn before it is written. It is meant for engineers who know some calculus, linear algebra and Python and have trained a neural network once; no reinforcement learning is assumed. Each lesson starts from a picture, adds one idea, and checks it with the results of an experiment that was actually run: a point mass, the heat, Burgers and Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equations, an airfoil in a gust with a CFD-built surrogate, and, in the last lesson, published studies of turbulence control. The airfoil experiments are written up in full as a flap controller trained inside a CFD-built surrogate and reduced-order models and a latent-space design search.

Where this lesson sits

This lesson has no learning algorithm in it yet. It sets up the stage on which every algorithm of the guide plays: something that acts, something that reacts, and one number that says how well it went.

Why control needs a third kind of learning

A network trained by supervised learning learns from simulations that were run beforehand and saved. Control cannot work that way, because the quality of an action only shows in how the system responds to it. Something must react to the controller while it learns, so an equation has to be solved inside the training loop.

In practice

To learn control, something must be controlled, and that means one equation to solve. Solving Navier–Stokes inside a training loop is too expensive for a first experiment, so the guide climbs through model equations: a point mass, the heat equation, Burgers, Kuramoto–Sivashinsky. This lesson uses the first one.

An old idea: trial and error with a direction

Reinforcement learning (RL) goes back to the beginnings of artificial intelligence in the 1950s, with Bellman as a key contributor. The idea is decision-making through interaction: try an action, see the score, prefer what scored well. Its fields of use include robotics, finance, games such as AlphaGo, and fluid mechanics.

Intuition

The objective is to maximize the reward, and the agent learns by trial and error. Because the reward points toward a goal, it is a very smart trial and error: the trials have a direction.

The loop

The agent is the thing that learns; in this guide it is a neural network. The environment is everything else: the physics, the solver, the sensors. Each action changes the state, which is the agent's observation of the system, and produces a reward, a scalar measure of the quality of the action.

StateWhat the controller observes: a position and a velocity, or a discretized field.
ActionWhat the controller changes: a force, or actuator amplitudes.
RewardHow good the action was: one number per step.
PolicyHow actions are selected from the state. Written π(a | s).
Key idea

These four words carry the whole vocabulary. Remember exactly these names, because every experiment in this guide is built from them.

What lives inside the two boxes

The loop above is the same in every lesson. What changes is what sits inside the two boxes. The drawing below opens them for the point mass: six slots inside the agent, five inside the environment, and the three arrows with the number of values each one carries. The same drawing returns in every later lesson with more slots switched on.

In this lesson the agent is almost empty. Its policy is any rule from state to action, its memory is the record of one episode, and nothing in it changes between episodes. The environment, on the other hand, is complete, and the next sections build it piece by piece. Lesson 3 fills the agent side: the policy becomes a network, and exploration, the update rule and the evaluation switch come with it. Lesson 3 also opens the network itself.

The same loop in three costumes

This is a ladder in which the physics becomes harder while the control vocabulary stays the same. In the channel the actions are blowing and suction at the wall, the state is the velocity fluctuation above the wall, and the reward is the relative reduction of the wall shear stress. Lessons 4 and 7 open the middle and the right panel; for the rest of this lesson the left one is enough.

The point mass, piece by piece

The point-mass experiment, the first experiment of this guide, uses the smallest possible plant. A unit mass slides on a line with some damping. The agent pushes it with a bounded force and must park it at the target position x★ = 1.

xk+1 = xk + Δt·vk     vk+1 = vk + Δt·(Fk − c·vk)     with Δt = 0.1, c = 0.2, 80 steps
StatePosition error and velocity.s = (x − x★, v)
ActionOne bounded force.a = F ∈ [−1, 1]
TransitionOne explicit Euler step of the two equations above.s′ = A·s + B·F
RewardMinus a cost: miss distance plus effort.r = −[(x − x★)² + 0.01·F²]

In CFD terms this is time stepping: the environment is a two-equation solver with explicit Euler, and one control step is one solver step. The best possible reward is zero, sitting on the target with no force. Every other situation scores negative, so "maximize reward" means get there, stay there, and do not waste effort.

The state stores the error x − x★ rather than x itself. This is on purpose: the target then always sits at zero error, so the same policy can serve another target later.

Feel the plant: push it yourself

Before any network, be the controller. The simulation below runs exactly the update above (Δt = 0.1, c = 0.2, x★ = 1, 80 steps, reward with weight 0.01 on F²). It opens on a simple demonstration: a constant force of +0.5 from x = −1.5.

Three things to try. First, the constant force: it carries the mass to the target and straight past it, and the summed reward ends worse than if you had not pushed at all (set F to 0 to compare). Second, "Push, then brake": tune the two sliders until the mass parks at x = 1, then press "New random start" and watch the same schedule miss. Third, the feedback rule, which reads the state at every step and parks the mass from any start.

Key idea

In one sentence: a constant open-loop force moves the mass toward the target but does not know when to brake, which is why the policy must use both position error and velocity. A schedule fixed in advance is open-loop control. A rule from state to action is feedback, and a policy is exactly such a rule.

The feedback rule in the third button is a proportional-derivative controller with gains 1.2 and 1.4. Lesson 3 treats it properly, next to the linear-quadratic regulator. Here it only shows what the agent has to discover by itself: push when far, brake when fast. From the standard start a well-tuned push-and-brake can score a little better than this rule (about −79 against −81), but it cannot repeat that from the next start.

The environment is a piece of software with two methods

An equation becomes an environment once it can be advanced by one control interval. reset() starts an episode and returns the first observation. step(action) applies one action, advances the dynamics by one control interval and returns five things: the new observation, the reward, a terminated flag, a truncated flag and a dictionary of diagnostics.

def step(self, action):
    force = float(np.clip(np.asarray(action).reshape(-1)[0], -1.0, 1.0))
    self.state = (self.A @ self.state + self.B[:, 0] * force).astype(np.float32)
    self.step_count += 1
    position_error, velocity = self.state
    reward = -(position_error**2 + self.effort_weight * force**2)
    terminated = False
    truncated = self.step_count >= self.horizon
    info = {"position": float(position_error + self.target),
            "velocity": float(velocity), "force": force}
    return (self.state.copy(), float(reward), terminated, truncated, info)

This is the step method of the PointMassEnv environment. Every line maps to a box you have already seen: clip the force, one Euler step as a matrix update, the reward, the two flags.

Four small functions share the work, and only the plant has a memory of its own: the two numbers in self.state. The observation here is a copy of exactly those two numbers, which is the simplest case; later environments measure less than the plant holds, and a variation of this experiment hides the velocity to see what that costs. The reward and the flags are computed fresh at every call from the state and the force. Nothing inside step() ever learns, and no gradient ever flows through it: from Lesson 3 on, learning happens outside, from the numbers it returns.

In practice

The environment is written by hand, but it follows the reset-and-step convention of the Gymnasium library on purpose. It is worth building one yourself once, because in a real problem the library may not be the right tool and you may have to do everything yourself. Lesson 5 moves the same point mass into Gymnasium.

How an episode ends, and where it starts

The distinction matters later. A truncated episode was cut by the clock, so the story would have continued; a terminated one really ended. The point-mass environment sets terminated = False always and truncated = True once the step count reaches the horizon of 80.

Random initial conditions keep the agent from memorizing one trajectory. With a single fixed start it could learn one sequence of pushes, the "Push, then brake" schedule you tuned above. With starts spread over the box it must learn a feedback law that works from anywhere in it.

In practice

The environment is created with a seed so that the random numbers are repeatable: the starts differ from episode to episode, but a rerun draws the same sequence and you can compare runs.

Reward scores a step, return scores what follows

A single reward measures only the immediate quality of one step. But a push now changes every later state, as the overshoot in the simulation above showed. So an action is judged by the return: the sum of the rewards from that step to the end of the episode, with later rewards counted a little less.

Gt = rt + γ·rt+1 + γ²·rt+2 + …  =  rt + γ·Gt+1

Read the bottom row from the left: G₀ = −7.34 is the score of the whole episode as seen from its first action, while G₃ = −1 only sees the last two steps. Early actions carry responsibility for everything that follows them. That is the right bookkeeping for a plant with inertia, where a push at step 5 decides where the mass is at step 40.

The discount factor sets how far ahead the agent looks

With γ near zero the controller looks only at the next step. Near one it weighs every step to the end of the episode and so considers long-term consequences. A rule of thumb: a discount factor near 0.99 makes the policy weigh long-term consequences, and lowering it to 0.95 makes the network focus on the next 10 to 20 steps.

The money picture

An analogy from finance: with γ = 0.9, a bill of 100 received one year later is worth 90 today. A reward that arrives later is worth less now, and γ is the exchange rate per step.

Why this is not a detail

The point-mass training run of Lesson 3 uses γ = 0.95 rather than 0.99. A good push on the point mass pays off tens of steps later, which a short-sighted agent hardly sees. Lesson 3 shows what that did to training.

The agent's whole objective in one sentence: find the policy whose expected return is as large as possible, where the expectation covers the random actions and the random starts. Every algorithm in the later lessons is a different way of chasing that one number.

The reward is the only channel for the goal

The reward is the only channel through which the objective reaches the policy, so its form decides what is learned. All four model environments of this guide (point mass, heat equation, Burgers, Kuramoto–Sivashinsky) use the same recipe, a negative cost with two parts: a tracking term (how far from the target) and an effort term (how hard the actuators work), weighted by λ. For the point mass λ = 0.01.

rk = −[ (1/ns)·‖sk+1 − s★‖² + λ·‖ak − a★‖² ]     point mass: r = −[(x − x★)² + 0.01·F²]
Pitfall

Some targets need a nonzero action just to be held. The heated rod of the heat-equation experiment (Lesson 4) keeps its target profile only while the heaters stay at a★ = (0.55, 0.35). Penalizing ‖a‖² there rewards the controller for switching off the very forcing that holds the target. Penalize the deviation ‖a − a★‖². The point mass escapes the problem because holding x = 1 needs no force, so a★ = 0.

The reward need not measure the objective directly. In the research of Lesson 7, a controller of wall turbulence was rewarded for suppressing the flow regions that an explainability method (SHAP) marked as most important, instead of for drag reduction itself. Lesson 7 returns to what that bought.

Exploring while training, committing when done

The agent learns by trying many different actions, stochastically, and training makes those with the highest return more probable. This is the balance between exploration (trying something new, which may be better) and exploitation (repeating what already works). Once training ends the parameters are frozen and the policy is evaluated deterministically: for a given state it always takes the same action.

The word "deep" means that the policy is a deep neural network. Because a network is nonlinear, it has an advantage precisely when the problem is difficult. How the network's weights are actually moved toward better actions is the policy gradient of Lesson 3.

Three difficulties built into the loop

First, the value of each state is not known in advance, which is why RL is trial and error in the first place. Second, exploration and exploitation must be balanced, and no rule settles that for every problem. Third, exploring costs simulation time, and for high-dimensional states and actions the learned quantities must be approximated with neural networks.

Each difficulty is answered by a later lesson. Lesson 2 defines "the value of a state" precisely. Lessons 3 to 5 show how different algorithms explore and how they reuse expensive experience. Lesson 7 shows what makes exploration affordable in a turbulent channel.

When is the learning worth it?

Learning does not beat classical control everywhere. For a known linear system with a quadratic objective, a classical regulator should normally be more accurate, more reliable and cheaper, and the point mass is such a system. It is a toy: it is there to show how the machinery works. Lessons 3 and 4 put the learned controller next to the proportional-derivative (PD) controller and the linear-quadratic regulator (LQR) on the same test cases.

Connect the dots

Everything hangs on the centre. The agent and the environment are the two boxes of the loop, the reward is the arrow that carries the goal, and the return is how rewards are added up along an episode. Exploration is what the agent does with the loop while it does not yet know better.

Check yourself

Why can't a controller be trained on a fixed dataset, the way a supervised network is?

Because nobody has the right action for each state, and the quality of an action only shows in how the system responds to it. Something must react to the controller while it learns, so the dataset is replaced by an environment: a simulation or an experiment.

Draw the loop and name its three arrows for the point mass.

Agent to environment: the action, one force F in [−1, 1]. Environment to agent: the next state (x − x★, v) and the reward −[(x − x★)² + 0.01·F²]. One turn is one explicit Euler step of Δt = 0.1.

A constant force of +0.5 from x = −1.5 ends with a worse summed reward than no force at all. Why, and what does a good controller need?

The open-loop force carries the mass through the target and far beyond it, because it does not know when to brake. Braking in time needs the velocity as well as the position error, which is why the state holds both and the policy must be a feedback rule.

Name the four components inside the environment box and say which of the five values returned by step() each one produces.

The plant (solver) advances the state s = (x − x★, v) by one Euler step and keeps it; it returns nothing directly. The observation returns a copy of that state, sₖ₊₁ (2 numbers). The reward function returns rₖ = −[(x − x★)² + 0.01·F²] (1 number). The end check returns terminated (always False) and truncated (True once the step count reaches 80). The info dictionary only carries diagnostics for plots.

Why would it be wrong to mark the end of every 80-step point-mass episode as terminated?

Nothing physical ended the episode; an outside step limit did. That is truncation. Termination is reserved for a physical or task condition, and the point-mass environment never sets it.

You lower γ from 0.99 to 0.95. What changes?

The agent becomes near-sighted. A reward 20 steps ahead drops from a weight of about 0.82 to about 0.36, so the network focuses on roughly the next 10 to 20 steps. On a plant where a good push pays off tens of steps later, that hides much of the consequence of each action.

The heaters must stay at a★ = (0.55, 0.35) to hold the target temperature profile. What goes wrong if the reward penalizes ‖a‖²?

The effort term is then lowest at a = 0, so the reward encourages the controller to switch off the forcing that holds the target. The best reward moves off the target. Penalizing ‖a − a★‖² puts both terms at zero in the same place.

Into Lesson 2

The return scores one episode after it has been played. Lesson 2 asks the sharper question: how good is it to be in a state, or to take a given action there, before the episode is played? The answer gives the value functions V and Q, the Markov property they rest on, and the Bellman equations, which grow directly out of the recursion Gt = rt + γ·Gt+1 you just worked by hand.

From Lesson 1

The return Gt = rt + γ·Gt+1 scores what followed an action in one episode, and the goal is the policy with the largest expected return. This lesson asks the next question: how good is it to be in a state, or to take a given action there, on average over many episodes?

One episode gives one return. A state deserves an average.

The policy samples its actions, so the same start gives a different trajectory and a different return each time. No single return is "the" score of that starting state. The stable quantity is the mean of all of them, and that mean is called the value of the state.

Vπ(s) = Eπ[ Gt | st = s ]

Read it aloud as "the return you expect from state s if policy π stays in control". Eπ is the average over everything random in the episodes that π generates.

Pitfall

A value always belongs to a policy. The superscript π is part of the definition: change the policy and the same state has a different value. "The value of this state" without saying which policy is controlling has no meaning.

The formal stage: a Markov decision process

To average over "everything that can follow", you need a precise description of what can follow. That description is the Markov decision process (MDP): the tuple (S, A, P, R) of states, actions, a transition function and a reward function.

P(s′ | s, a) = Pr( st+1 = s′ | st = s, at = a )     rt = R(st, at, st+1)
S, the state spaceAll states the system can be in. Here two; for the heat-equation experiment, every possible temperature field on the grid.
A, the action spaceAll actions the agent may take. Here two; in the experiments of this guide a continuous force or actuator amplitude.
P, the transition functionThe probability that action a in state s leads to s′. It is the physics.
R, the reward functionThe number assigned to each transition (s, a, s′). It is the objective.

The blue arrows are the agent's part: the policy π(a | s) decides which action node is entered. The green arrows are the environment's part. Every expectation in this lesson is an average over those two kinds of arrow, blue then green.

In practice

Before any learning, the control problem must be expressed as a Markov decision process, defined by a state, an action, a transition rule and a reward. These four things have to be defined every time a problem like this is set up, as they are for the heat-equation experiment.

The Markov property: the present state is enough

This is the Markov property, and it sits inside the conditioning of P(s′ | s, a): only s and a appear, no earlier history. In CFD terms, it is what makes restarting a simulation from a saved field possible. One honest caveat from the solver side: a multi-step scheme that stores earlier time levels needs those levels too, so there the "state" is the current field together with the stored ones.

Intuition

For the heat equation the state contains all the information required to compute the next temperature field: what happens at step k+1 is fixed by the state and the action at step k, and does not depend on whatever happened before.

Where the property breaks: sensors see only part of the state

This matters in practice: the measured state of a real system is often only a partial observation of a higher-dimensional state. It returns in the channel-flow research, where the agent sees one plane of the flow and the authors note that the system is then "not entirely Markovian" (Lesson 7). The Kuramoto–Sivashinsky (KS) experiment with only eight sensor points tests exactly this limit; Lesson 5 covers it.

Deterministic solver, random episodes

The MDP is written with probabilities so that it also covers noisy systems. The point-mass, heat-equation, Burgers and Kuramoto–Sivashinsky environments of this guide advance by a numerical time step, which returns the same next state for the same state and action. The expectation in the objective therefore covers the random actions and the random initial conditions.

Three numbers for one state: V, Q and the advantage

V judges a state. To judge an action, fix the first action and let the policy take over afterwards. That gives the action-value function, or Q function. The difference between the two is the advantage.

Vπ(s) = Eπ[Gt | st=s]     Qπ(s,a) = Eπ[Gt | st=s, at=a]     Aπ(s,a) = Qπ(s,a) − Vπ(s)
Vπ(s) = Σa π(a|s) · Qπ(s,a)    ⇒    Σa π(a|s) · Aπ(s,a) = 0

Averaging Q over the policy's own actions gives back V. So the advantages, weighted the same way, always sum to zero: the readout under the chart stays at 0.00 wherever the slider is. The advantage answers a relative question, "is this action better or worse than what the policy would do on average here?", and that relative question is the one the learning algorithms of Lessons 3 and 4 need.

Where V and Q live in the loop

The value functions are not a new box in the environment. They sit inside the agent, next to the policy, and they are built from what the loop delivers: the observations and rewards that pass through Memory. That placement is the anatomy of every actor–critic method later in the guide; only the table inside the critic slot becomes a network.

The Bellman expectation equation: a state's value from its successors

Computing V from its definition would mean summing rewards over every possible future. The recursion of the return, Gt = rt + γ·Gt+1, removes that need: take one step, collect one reward, and what remains is the value of where you landed.

Vπ(s) = Σa π(a|s) Σs′ P(s′|s,a) [ R(s,a,s′) + γ·Vπ(s′) ]
  1. π(a|s): average over the actions the policy might take (blue branches).
  2. P(s′|s,a): for each action, average over where the environment might send you (green branches).
  3. R + γ·Vπ(s′): on each branch, the reward of that one step plus the discounted value of the landing state.

What this achieves: the equation replaces a sum over all future time steps by a relation between the value of a state and the values of its successors, which is what makes the value computable. The same recursion holds for Q, with the action fixed at the top and the policy averaging at the next state.

The same shape as an iterative linear solver

For a fixed policy the Bellman expectation equation is a linear system: one equation per state, each coupling a state to its successors. Iterating it from any initial guess converges to Vπ; this is called policy evaluation, and it is a fixed-point iteration of the same kind as Jacobi sweeps. The analogy has limits you should keep in mind: the "neighbours" are successor states under the dynamics, which need not be near each other in physical space, and it is the discount γ < 1 that makes each sweep shrink the error.

The Bellman optimality equation: replace the average by a maximum

Define the best achievable values as V*(s) = maxπ Vπ(s) and Q*(s,a) = maxπ Qπ(s,a). They satisfy the same recursion, with the average over actions replaced by a maximum.

V*(s) = maxa Σs′ P(s′|s,a) [ R(s,a,s′) + γ·V*(s′) ]
Q*(s,a) = Σs′ P(s′|s,a) [ R(s,a,s′) + γ·maxa′ Q*(s′,a′) ]     π*(s) = argmaxa Q*(s,a)
Key idea

Bellman's principle of optimality: a multi-step policy that is optimal overall must be optimal from every state it reaches. So the best long plan can be assembled from best single steps, provided each step is judged by reward plus the optimal value of where it lands. If Q* is known, the best action in a state is the one with the largest Q*.

Intuition

Reinforcement learning goes back to the 1950s, the very beginning of artificial intelligence, and Bellman founded this part of it. "Deep" reinforcement learning is the same idea with a deep neural network doing the learning.

Watch the values spread: value iteration, one sweep at a time

A small grid makes both Bellman equations visible. The agent moves one cell up, down, left or right; a move into a wall or the edge leaves it where it is. Entering the goal pays +1, entering the pit pays −1, both end the episode, and every other move pays 0.

Press Reset, then Sweep several times. After one sweep only the cell next to the goal knows anything. Each further sweep carries the information one cell further back, multiplied by γ, exactly as the backup diagram says: a cell's value is built from its successors' values. Lower γ and the values fade faster with distance; the arrows, however, still find the goal.

Now switch to the random policy. The same cells get much lower values, negative near the pit, because a policy that stumbles around often falls in. That is the pitfall from the first section made visible: value is a property of a state under a policy. With the arrows on in this mode you see the greedy policy with respect to Vπ, which is already far better than the random policy that produced those values.

Look at the residual chart too. Under the random policy the largest change falls geometrically, like the residual of a linear solver. This grid has 19 cells to solve for and a known model; flow problems have continuous states and no table can hold their values, which is where the neural networks of the later lessons come in.

Two ways to organize the sweeps: policy iteration and value iteration

You ran both in the grid. "Evaluate the random policy" followed by turning the arrows on is one round of the left chart: evaluate, then improve greedily. "Max" mode is the right chart. Both are dynamic programming: they sweep over all states and they use P and R directly in every update.

Why Q is the more useful table when the model is unknown

This is the practical meaning of π*(s) = argmaxa Q*(s,a). In the grid the arrows were drawn by looking one cell ahead, which was possible because the grid's rules were known. An agent that cannot query the rules cannot do that from V alone. The takeaway in one clause: Q* yields the optimal policy without a model.

The solver is the model, and nobody hands it to the agent

Methods that use or learn a model of the dynamics are called model-based; the others are model-free. A turbulent flow has no table of P(s′ | s, a): its transitions come out of a Navier–Stokes solver, one at a time, so the agent must learn from samples of interaction. The flow-control studies discussed in this guide are model-free; the channel-flow controller of Lesson 7, for example, is a model-free off-policy actor–critic. The experiments of this guide are model-free in the same sense: the policy network never sees the equations inside the environment.

Inside the agent: the one slot that differs

Everything about model-based versus model-free is in that one slot. With P and R inside, the update rule can run the exact backup for any state, visited or not, which is how the grid was solved. Without them, the update rule can only use the transitions in Memory, and the exact sum over s′ becomes an average over what the solver happened to return.

A Bellman backup computed from Memory

This is the model-free form of the backup diagram from earlier in the lesson. The branches weighted by P(s′ | s, a) are gone, because the agent never had P; in their place stands a single leaf, the s′ that the solver actually returned. One such sample is a noisy estimate of the exact backup, and the average over many rows approaches it. Q-learning (Lesson 5) does exactly this with the target r + γ·maxa′ Q(s′, a′), and the critics of Lesson 4 do it with a network in place of the table.

Key idea

The Bellman equations stay true when the model is unknown. What changes is how they are used: the exact sums over P are replaced by averages over sampled transitions, and the tables V and Q are replaced by neural networks.

The fork in the road: two routes and their combination

The names are all you need for now. Lesson 3 takes the policy-based branch with REINFORCE on the point mass. Lesson 4 adds the critic for the heat, Burgers and Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equations. Lesson 5 lays out DQN, DDPG, TD3 and PPO and where each one sits on this tree.

Preview: how the advantage will steer the policy

Compare this with the definition A = Q − V. The actor–critic experiments of this guide use the observed return Gk in place of Qπ(sk, ak), which is a single-sample estimate of it, and a learned network V in place of Vπ. How that critic is trained is Lesson 4's subject.

Rule of thumb

The actor should not reinforce every action equally. If Ak is greater than zero the outcome was better than the critic predicted; if it is less than zero the outcome was worse than expected, so that action should become less probable.

Connect the dots

Read it from the top. One episode gives a return; averaging returns gives V and Q; the MDP's structure turns those averages into the Bellman equations; with a known model the equations are solved by sweeping; without one, the same equations are satisfied approximately from samples, along one of three families of algorithms.

Check yourself

Two people quote different values for the same state of the point mass. Can both be right?

Yes, if they have different policies in mind. Vπ(s) is the expected return from s while π stays in control. In the grid, the same cell is worth far less under the random policy than under the optimal one.

In a state with three actions the policy's probabilities are 0.2, 0.5, 0.3 and Q is 4, 7, 1. What are V and the three advantages?

V = 0.2·4 + 0.5·7 + 0.3·1 = 4.6. The advantages are Q − V: −0.6, +2.4 and −3.6. Weighted by the policy they sum to 0.2·(−0.6) + 0.5·2.4 + 0.3·(−3.6) = 0, as they always do.

The solver advances the field deterministically. Why does the value still need an expectation?

Because the episodes are still random. In the experiments of this guide the start state is drawn at reset and the policy samples its actions during training, so the same policy produces a spread of returns.

What single change turns the Bellman expectation equation into the optimality equation, and what does it mean?

The average over actions, weighted by π(a|s), becomes a maximum over actions. It means "assume the best action is taken here and from every later state", which is Bellman's principle of optimality.

You are handed a perfect V* for a flow-control problem, but no model. Why can you still not act optimally, and what would fix it?

Picking the best action from V* needs a one-step look-ahead: where does each action land, and what is V* there? That requires P. With Q* instead, the look-ahead is already inside each number and the best action is the argmax over a.

In the anatomy loop, which slot separates a model-based agent from a model-free one, and what does the model-free agent use instead?

The slot for a model of the environment, P and R, inside the agent. A model-based agent holds it (the grid's known rules) and can sweep every state. In a model-free agent that slot is empty, so the update rule works from the transitions (s, a, r, s′) in Memory: the one s′ that happened stands in for the sum over P, and the average over many rows approaches the exact backup.

An agent sees eight sensor readings of a 64-point field. Which assumption of this lesson is at risk?

The Markov property. Different full fields can give the same eight readings and then evolve differently, so the observation no longer fixes the future. This is called partial observation; Lesson 5 returns to the sensor-limited experiments.

Into Lesson 3

You now have the yardsticks: V, Q, the advantage and the equations that tie them together. But the grid was solved by sweeping a table with the model in hand. The point mass has continuous states and forces, so there is no table to sweep, and the agent is not shown the equations of its environment. Lesson 3 takes the policy-based route: how can a network that only outputs a probability distribution over forces be improved using nothing more than the returns of its own episodes? That is REINFORCE, on the point-mass experiment.

Lesson 3 of 7 · The point-mass experiment

Policy gradients with REINFORCE

After this lesson you can explain, with pictures, how returns nudge a neural network policy, why the simplest way of doing it is noisy, and how the learned controller is judged against the classical PD and LQR controllers.

From Lesson 2

Lesson 2 ended at a fork. One route learns a value function and reads the policy off it. The other route adjusts the policy itself. This lesson takes the second route in its simplest form, on the point-mass experiment, a mass on a line that a bounded force must bring to a target position: same loop, reward, return and discount as in Lesson 1.

Before training a network, build the classical yardsticks

A learned controller means little without something to measure it against. The point-mass experiment starts by building two classical controllers. Both read the same state as the agent: the position error e = x − x★ and the velocity v.

PD:  F = −kp·e − kd·v,  clipped to [−1, 1]
LQR:  F = −K·s,  K = (R + BᵀPB)⁻¹ BᵀPA

Standard LQR knows nothing about the force limit. Once its output is clipped to ±1 it is no longer the exact optimum, but it stays a very strong reference. Solving the Riccati equation costs O(n³) in the number of states, which is trivial here with two states and becomes a real cost for large fields.

Rule of thumb

Implement a classical reference before training a neural controller, and compare them only on the same plant, cost, constraints and distribution of initial conditions. The baseline stops you from crediting the network for behaviour that standard control obtains more simply.

Try both controllers on the point mass

Look at the force panel. LQR pushes at the limit for a long stretch, then reverses hard to brake, so it arrives first. PD pushes more gently and arrives later. Without any force the mass only coasts on its initial velocity and the cost piles up.

In practice

PD is smoother, LQR is faster, and LQR is on the target in about 40 steps. Classical control is not the aim of this lesson. These two curves are the yardstick for what follows.

What each controller needs and what it promises

For a known linear system with a quadratic objective, LQR should normally be more accurate, more reliable and cheaper than any learned policy. The case for learning grows with nonlinear dynamics, missing models, incomplete observations, non-quadratic rewards and complicated actuator limits. The point mass has none of these, so here the network is the student and LQR is the answer key.

The anatomy of the learner: which component sits where

The loop of Lesson 1 is the same for every method in this guide. What changes from method to method is what sits inside the two boxes. Below is the REINFORCE learner of the point-mass experiment with every component in its slot. Click a slot, or tab to it and press Enter, to read what it holds here, what goes in and out, and the code it corresponds to. The sections that follow open the lit slots one at a time.

Two things in the picture deserve a second look. The reward and the observation do not go straight to the update: they are written into the memory of the episode first, and only after 80 steps does the update rule read the memory once. And every dashed arrow stays inside the agent box. Weights change only on the left; the simulator on the right is called like any function and is never differentiated.

The policy: a network that places a bell curve over the force

The block diagram shows the path of the data. The next drawing opens the blocks and shows the neurons and the weights themselves, so that "1,185 weights" becomes something you can count.

So "the policy outputs a distribution" has a concrete meaning here. For every state the network says where the bell sits, and one extra parameter says how wide it is. The output layer starts at zero, so the untrained policy applies zero force on average. The inputs are divided by fixed numbers (3 and 2) so both arrive at the network with similar size.

Why tanh and not a hard clip? A force of 20 would throw the mass far past the target, so the force must be bounded, and tanh bounds it smoothly, which backpropagation needs. A clip would also pile probability at exactly ±1, which a Gaussian log-probability does not describe.

Same state, different pushes: σ is the exploration knob

With a small σ every push is nearly the same and the agent learns nothing new. With a large σ the pushes cover the whole range and pile up near ±1, and the agent can hardly tell which of them helped. Training needs something in between, and training lets the optimizer adjust σ within the clipping bounds. A small entropy bonus (weight 10⁻⁴) discourages σ from collapsing too early.

The log-probability: how strongly the policy backed its own action

log πθ(Ft | st) = log N(yt; μθ(st), σ²) − log(1 − tanh² yt)

The first term is the height of the bell at the raw sample y. The second term is the correction for the tanh squashing: tanh compresses the axis near ±1, which changes the density, and the change-of-variables formula accounts for it. This is why training records the raw sample y of every step and not only the force.

The REINFORCE principle: the return decides which actions to back

Actions followed by a good return become more probable. Actions followed by a poor return become less probable. That is the whole method.

∇θ J(θ) ≈ (1/T) · Σt  Gt · ∇θ log πθ(at | st)
in practice the weight is Ĝt = (Gt − mean G) / (std G + ε)
∇θ log πθ(at|st)The direction in weight space that makes the action taken at step t more probable.
GtThe return that followed that action (Lesson 1): how far to go in that direction, and with which sign.
(1/T) · ΣtThe average over the T = 80 steps of the one episode just played.
What is missingAny derivative of the environment. The simulator can be a black box; only the network's log-probability is differentiated.

In this experiment the returns are first centred and scaled within the episode. Without that step every weight would be negative, because every reward of the point mass is negative, and the update would push down on every sampled action. After centring, the steps that did better than this episode's average get a positive weight and are pushed up.

Watch the mechanism: one state, many samples, repeated updates

Press Update several times. The amber dots sit mostly on one side of the mean, so the average of the weighted arrows points that way and the bell walks toward the best action. Near the best action the amber dots surround the mean on both sides and the steps become small and erratic. Switch on "Also learn σ" and the bell narrows once the good samples are the ones close to the mean.

Key idea

The policy never sees the rule that scores the actions. It only sees which of its own samples did better than average, and shifts probability toward them. Replace "toy rule" by "80 steps of a simulator" and you have REINFORCE.

One training iteration, message by message

The stage in the middle deserves its own picture. The chart below runs the untrained policy's mean action (zero force) from test start 0 with the experiment's equations and shows what the return computation does to the 80 rewards.

Notice the tail of panel 2. The return climbs toward zero at the end simply because fewer negative rewards remain to be summed, whatever the actions were. The per-episode mean cannot tell "a good action" from "an easy position in the episode". In general terms, this normalisation is a practical heuristic that modifies the estimator and may bias it.

# one REINFORCE update from a complete episode (shortened)
weights = (returns - returns.mean()) / (returns.std() + 1e-8)
with tf.GradientTape() as tape:
    means = reinforce_policy(states_t, training=True)
    log_probabilities = squashed_log_prob(raw_actions_t, means, reinforce_log_std)
    loss = -tf.reduce_mean(log_probabilities * weights_t)
    entropy = tf.reduce_sum(reinforce_log_std + 0.5 * (1.0 + np.log(2.0 * np.pi)))
    loss -= 1e-4 * entropy
variables = reinforce_policy.trainable_variables + [reinforce_log_std]
gradients = tape.gradient(loss, variables)
reinforce_optimizer.apply_gradients(zip(gradients, variables))
reinforce_log_std.assign(tf.clip_by_value(reinforce_log_std, -3.0, 0.5))

The minus sign in the loss is there because optimizers minimise and the agent wants to maximise. The means are recomputed inside the tape so that the loss is connected to the weights; the recorded samples and the weights enter as plain numbers.

The same update once more, this time as arrays. Reading the shapes on the arrows tells you where the forward passes happen, where the single backward pass happens, and that the two never meet inside the simulator.

Why the estimate is noisy, and what the fixes are

Monte Carlo returnThe weight Gt is the sum of up to 80 rewards along one random trajectory. It is an estimate from samples, with all the scatter of those samples.
One episode per updateNothing is averaged over several episodes before the weights move.
Random startA start far from the target gives poor returns whatever the policy does. That scatter enters the weights too.
Noise on every action80 random draws per episode; the return of step t also depends on the luck of all later steps.

There are two fixes. The first is the one used here: centre and scale the returns within the episode. The second is a baseline: subtract from each return what was to be expected anyway, so that only "better or worse than expected" is left. Subtracting a baseline lowers the variance without changing which actions look better.

The scatter between starts is large on this problem. Even for LQR, the cost over the 50 test starts runs from 0.02 to 125.8, with a mean of 22.5. A baseline that knows the state would remove that part of the noise. You met its definition in Lesson 2 as V(s), and return minus V is the advantage; the network that learns V is the critic of Lesson 4.

What happened in training

This is the variance of the previous section, visible in an actual training run. The exploration width barely moved: σ started near 0.497 and stayed between 0.488 and 0.503 through run B. A σ that never shrinks says the policy has not committed to a behaviour.

In practice

The discount factor is a setting to check. In an informal trial with γ = 0.99 the policy seemed to have the idea of the task after about 200 episodes. With γ = 0.95, the value used in all runs shown here, the mean return collapses at episode 100. No run compares the two values side by side, so the effect of γ is an observation and not a measured result.

What a control law looks like: force as a map over the state

The LQR gain is so high that its plane is cut off almost everywhere. Far from the target it acts like a switch: full push, then full brake once the path crosses the thin band, then a short linear landing. PD has a wide linear band and a gentler path.

The learned policy is a third map of the same kind, F = tanh(μθ(e, v)), a curved surface where PD and LQR have a plane. A well-trained policy on this problem would have to resemble the two pictures above: positive on the left, negative on the right, with a braking tilt in v. The snapshot described above shows that, on test start 0 at least, run C ended on the wrong side of it.

Judging the result: five rules, then the numbers

Who wins? LQR, in every run, as it should on a known linear system with a quadratic cost. PD is a close second. REINFORCE comes third at best. In run A it is within 11% of LQR; in runs B and C it is roughly 20 to 30 times worse. Three runs do not measure the run-to-run spread, but they show it is large.

This is why the common test matters. A difference of 1.4 between two means with standard deviations of 32 looks like nothing. Paired on the same starts it is a consistent advantage. One plotted trajectory would have shown neither fact.

Rule of thumb

Single test cases tell different stories. From one start REINFORCE can look not so bad; from a start at x ≈ 1.6 with negative velocity it does poorly. Always run 50 to 80 realisations from different initial conditions, never one.

What this experiment shows, and its pitfalls

The point-mass experiment supports two conclusions: REINFORCE does learn continuous feedback without differentiating the environment, and its Monte Carlo gradient has substantial variance. The two questions below add what to check when the learned controller loses.

QuestionAnswer
Why does REINFORCE lose to PD and LQR here, and what should be changed?LQR is the optimum for this problem and PD is already very good, so a learned policy is not expected to win. Its poor trajectories come from choices to be checked one by one: discount factor, number of episodes, network size, exploration, return normalisation.
Can early stopping be used?In an adapted form. There is no dataset to overfit; the budget of episodes plays that role. The actor–critic experiments of Lesson 4 score the deterministic policy on fixed validation starts during training and keep the best one. The point-mass experiment has no such step: the policy after episode 400 is the one tested.
Pitfall: the discount factor

A value inside the usual range can still be too short-sighted. With γ = 0.95 a reward 20 steps ahead counts 0.36; with 0.99 it counts 0.82. On this problem a good push pays off tens of steps later: from test start 0 even LQR needs 42 steps to settle. Check the value in the code, not the comment beside it.

Pitfall: clipping the action instead of squashing it

A clipped Gaussian sample piles probability at exactly ±1, which the Gaussian log-probability does not represent, and a clip has no useful gradient there. Squash with tanh and include the correction term in log π.

Pitfall: comparing on different terms

Compare controllers only on the same plant, the same cost, the same force limit and the same starts. Note one subtlety in this experiment: the LQR was designed with a small extra weight on velocity (Q = diag(1, 0.05)) and an infinite horizon, which is not exactly the reward. The comparison stays fair because all three controllers are scored with the same cost, the summed negative reward over 80 steps.

Pitfall: trusting one training run

Run A gives 25.05 for REINFORCE, run B 483.60 and run C 681.63. Judge a learned controller on many test starts and, where you can, on more than one training run. The learning rate (2 × 10⁻³), the number of episodes (400) and the exploration width are the other settings worth varying; none of them was varied in this experiment.

Connect the dots

Put in one sentence: a network places a bell curve over the force, the episode's returns say which sampled forces to make more likely, and one gradient step per episode moves the weights that way. Everything else on the map is there to keep that simple learner honest: classical controllers to measure against, a fair test, and an open eye for the variance that the next lesson attacks.

Check yourself

The policy network of this lesson has one output. What is it, and where does the randomness come from?

The output is the mean μ(s) of a Gaussian. The width σ is one separate trainable number, kept as log σ. During training a raw sample y = μ + σ·ε is drawn and squashed to F = tanh(y); in evaluation the noise is dropped and F = tanh(μ).

All rewards of the point mass are negative. What would the update do without return normalisation?

Every weight Gt would be negative, so the update would lower the probability of every sampled action, by more where the return was worse. After centring within the episode, the steps with an above-average return get a positive weight and are made more probable.

Name the three arrays that one episode leaves in memory, with their shapes, and say which numbers of the whole update receive a gradient.

States 80 × 2, raw samples y 80 and rewards 80. The gradient exists only for the 1,185 network weights and the one log σ, computed inside the gradient tape from the batched forward pass. The returns enter as plain numbers and the simulator is only called, never differentiated.

Why can REINFORCE train on a solver whose equations the network never sees?

Only the log-probability computed by the network is differentiated. The environment supplies states and rewards as plain numbers, so it can be any simulation or black box. This is what lets the same learner move to PDE solvers in Lesson 4.

Name three sources of the high variance of the REINFORCE gradient.

The weights are Monte Carlo returns summed along one random trajectory; only one episode is used per update; each episode starts from a random state that shifts all its returns; and every one of the 80 actions carries its own noise.

PD and LQR differ by about 1.4 in mean cost, and each has a standard deviation above 32. Why is the difference still meaningful?

Both controllers run from exactly the same 50 starts. The large standard deviation comes from the starts differing in difficulty. Paired start by start, LQR is cheaper in all 50 cases, by between 0.02 and 2.15.

Run A scores 25.05 for REINFORCE and run B, with the same code and seeds, 483.60. What can you conclude?

That the result of run A was not reproduced by a repeat of the same code and seeds, and that the method's outcome varies strongly from run to run. Run C gave 681.63. Three runs do not identify a cause and do not measure the spread; they do show that one training run is not enough to trust.

Into Lesson 4

REINFORCE struggles on a system with two states. The next system has 39: the temperatures of a discretised heat equation, then the Burgers and Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equations. The same learner needs help to cope, and the help is the baseline from this lesson turned into a second network. How does a critic learn "what was expected", and what does it buy on a PDE?

One learner is carried up three equations of rising difficulty. From Lesson 3

REINFORCE worked on the two-state point mass, but its updates were noisy: every action was weighted by the raw return of the whole episode that followed it. This lesson fixes that with a second network, the critic, and then asks the engineering question. Does the same learner still work when the environment is a PDE solver with 39 or 64 states?

One learner, four rungs of physics

The experiments are built so that only one thing changes at a time. From the heat-equation experiment (two heaters on a rod) to the Burgers experiment (two actuators on a field that carries itself) to the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky (KS) experiment (five actuators on a chaotic field), the learner is kept and the physics is exchanged. That makes the three experiments comparable, and it is why this lesson spends as much time on the solvers as on the learner.

KS stands for the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation, the chaotic model equation closest to Navier–Stokes in this guide. PDE stands for partial differential equation.

What is wrong with weighting by the raw return?

REINFORCE multiplies the log-probability of each action by the return that followed it (Lesson 3 has the mechanics). The trouble is that most of a return is explained by where the episode started. An episode that starts far from the target collects a large cost whatever the actions were.

Aₖ = Gₖ − V(sₖ)
Aₖ > 0: better than the critic predicted, make the action more probable
Aₖ < 0: worse than predicted, make it less probable

The critic is a network that predicts the return expected from a state while the actor keeps control. The advantage is the observed return minus that prediction. The question changes from "was the outcome good in absolute terms?" to "was it better than expected from here?". Switch the figure between the two modes and watch the arrows of episode B: with raw returns nearly all of them point up, although half of those actions did worse than expected for their state.

Key idea

The critic is a learned, state-dependent baseline. It removes from the return the part that the state alone explains. What is left is the part the action is responsible for, and that part has far less variance.

Two networks: one acts, one judges

Before the two networks are opened up, here is where they sit in the loop. The actor fills the Policy slot and the critic fills the slot that Lessons 1 to 3 left empty. Both read the same observation, the whole field. Only the actor's output leaves the agent; the critic's output never reaches the environment, it is used inside the Update rule only.

The actor is the stochastic policy of Lesson 3: a Gaussian sample squashed by tanh into (−1, 1). New here is that it learns a correction Δμ to the action a★ that holds the target, so training starts from a physically sensible controller instead of an arbitrary saturated one. The critic has the same body and one output. For KS the layers are 96 wide (16,037 and 15,649 weights), the outputs are five action means and one value, the learning rates are 2·10⁻⁴ and 8·10⁻⁴, and log σ starts at −0.7.

V(sₖ) ≈ E[ Σj ≥ k γj−k rj | sₖ ]   ·   γ = 0.99

Read the two losses term by term. The critic loss pulls V(s) toward the observed returns G; the Huber form is quadratic for small errors and linear for large ones, so a few very bad episodes do not dominate. In the actor loss, log π is the only quantity differentiated, Â is a fixed number per step (the critic is frozen with a stop-gradient), and the small entropy term rewards keeping the action distribution spread out.

Intuition

The actor does something, the critic checks. It resembles the two networks of a generative adversarial network, where one produces and the other judges and both improve by training together. It is similar, not the same.

Inside the actor and the critic

Count the weights to see the sizes: a dense layer from n inputs to m units holds n·m weights and m biases. For the heat and Burgers actor the three layers hold 6,850 weights, and the two entries of log σ are trained alongside them; the critic's trunk is the same size and its single output brings it to 6,785. On KS the layers are 96 wide, the input has 64 values and the output five, which gives 16,037 + 5 and 15,649. Nothing else in the learner changes between the experiments.

Two details of the output head matter. The noise is added before the tanh, so the sampled action can never leave the actuator bounds, and the log-probability used in the loss carries a correction for that squashing. And because log σ is a free parameter rather than a network output, the exploration level is the same in every state and changes only when the update moves it.

One batched update, stage by stage

Each update pools eight episodes from eight random starting profiles: 8 × 120 = 960 steps for heat and Burgers. One trajectory is a poor basis for an update, because it tells the learner about one start only. Averaging the gradient over eight starts makes it more representative, which lowers the noise a second time, on top of the critic's baseline.

The critic gets five passes per batch and the actor one small, clipped step. The order matters: the critic is fitted to the new returns first, then frozen, and only then used as the baseline for the actor.

The sequence diagram says who talks to whom; the figure below says what the arrays look like at each stage. Both tell the same story: everything the environment produces is data, and the only quantities that are differentiated are the two losses, each a single number computed from the networks’ outputs.

# one update of the Burgers experiment (trimmed)
states, raw_actions, returns, _ = collect_batch(env, episodes_per_batch)   # 8 episodes

for _ in range(critic_passes):                                # 5 passes
    with tf.GradientTape() as tape:
        values = tf.squeeze(critic(states_t, training=True), axis=1)
        critic_loss = huber(returns_t, values)
    ...apply critic gradients...

baseline   = tf.stop_gradient(tf.squeeze(critic(states_t, training=False), axis=1))
advantages = returns_t - baseline
advantages = (advantages - tf.reduce_mean(advantages)) / (tf.math.reduce_std(advantages) + 1e-8)

with tf.GradientTape() as tape:
    corrections = actor(states_t, training=True)
    log_probs   = squashed_gaussian_log_prob(raw_t, corrections)
    actor_loss  = -tf.reduce_mean(log_probs * advantages)
    actor_loss -= 1e-4 * entropy
...apply actor gradients, clip log_std to [-2.5, -0.3]...

This is an introductory Monte Carlo actor–critic: complete returns, no replay buffer, no target network, no one-step bootstrapped target. Those devices belong to the library algorithms of Lesson 5.

In practice

Training two networks takes time, and how much depends on the machine. The heat-equation training run shown here took 162 s. On a slower machine the same run took 14 minutes.

How a PDE solver becomes an environment

An environment is a class with two methods. reset starts an episode from a random initial condition. step applies one action, advances the dynamics by one control interval, and returns the new state, the reward, a terminated flag, a truncated flag and diagnostics. In all three PDE experiments the episode is truncated at a fixed horizon and never terminated.

CFD already keeps two time scales apart: the output interval and the solver time step. Here the control interval plays the role of the output interval. Changing one should never silently change the other.

HeatBurgersKuramoto–Sivashinsky
Equationut = α uxx + Σ ajφjut + (u²/2)x = ν uxx + Σ ajφjut + u ux + uxx + uxxxx = Σ ajφj
Domain0 < x < 1, walls at 00 < x < 1, walls at 0periodic, length ℓ = 22
State39 interior temperatures39 interior velocities64 periodic values
Actuators2 Gaussian heaters at x = 0.3, 0.7, width 0.082 Gaussian actuators at x = 0.3, 0.7, width 0.085 periodic Gaussians, width 1.0, mean removed
Parameterα = 0.05ν = 0.02none (ℓ sets the dynamics)
Time integrationimplicit Euler, central differencesRusanov flux, adaptive explicit Euler substepsFourier spectral, ETDRK4, two-thirds dealiasing
Control step, episode0.05, 120 steps0.05, 120 steps1.0, 80 steps
Targets★ held by a★ = (0.55, 0.35)s★ held by a★ = (0.45, 0.30)u★ = 0 with a★ = 0, unstable
Effort weight λ0.020.020.01
Pitfall

The solver is part of the learning problem. A numerically unstable or biased environment teaches the wrong control problem, so physical fidelity and training stability cannot be separated. Verify the solver before training anything on it.

Environment 1: the heat equation, live

A rod with both ends held at zero temperature and two Gaussian heaters. Central differences on 41 grid points turn the PDE into 39 coupled ordinary differential equations, ds/dt = L s + Φ a. One implicit Euler step over the control interval then gives the same linear form as the point mass, only with bigger matrices.

(I − Δt L) sk+1 = sk + Δt Φ ak  →  sk+1 = A sk + B ak
A is 39 × 39, B is 39 × 2, spectral radius of A = 0.976

Press Play and move the sliders: you are the policy now, and the cost readout is the negative of the return. Then replay the same start with Hold a★ and with LQR drives. LQR pushes both heaters to the limit for the first steps and then relaxes to a★, which is what the classical optimum does on this plant.

In practice

The heat equation is closer to flow simulation than it looks: solving Navier–Stokes amounts largely to solving many heat equations. And the inverse in A = (I − Δt L)⁻¹ is notation. You never compute an inverse; you solve the linear system.

Why the target must be reachable

Heat: s★ = (I − A)⁻¹ B a★,   a★ = (0.55, 0.35)
Burgers: integrate with a★ = (0.45, 0.30) until max|Δs| < 10⁻⁸

Two narrow heaters cannot hold an arbitrary temperature profile. If the target is drawn by hand, the leftover error would be blamed on the learner although no controller could remove it. So the experiments turn the order around: pick a constant action a★, let the physics say which steady profile s★ it sustains, and use that pair as the target. In the live figure above, set a₂ = 0 and try to build a peak at x = 0.7 to feel this.

rₖ = −[ ‖sk+1 − s★‖² / ns + λ ‖aₖ − a★‖² ]
λ = 0.02 (heat, Burgers), 0.01 (KS, where s★ = 0 and a★ = 0)

The reward is written in deviation variables. The first term is the mean squared distance from the target after the step. The second charges for effort measured from the holding action. The best possible reward is zero, reached exactly at the target with a = a★.

Pitfall

Penalising ‖a‖² instead of ‖a − a★‖² when the target needs a nonzero holding action. The reward then pays the controller for switching off the very forcing that holds the target.

Environment 2: Burgers, where the field carries itself

The viscous Burgers equation is a one-dimensional relative of Navier–Stokes. Its nonlinear term transports the field at a speed equal to the field's own value, which steepens it; viscosity ν = 0.02 smooths the smallest scales. The term is written in flux form, ∂(u²/2)/∂x, because a finite-volume scheme balances fluxes between cells, and a Rusanov (local Lax–Friedrichs) interface flux stays robust near steep fronts.

Δtsub = 0.45 / ( max|u| / Δx + 2ν / Δx² )
near the target: 0.45 / (19.9 + 64) ≈ 0.0054, so 10 substeps per interval

Readers with a CFD background will recognise the step-size rule. The first term in the bracket is the advective (CFL) limit, the second the diffusive limit, and 0.45 is the safety factor. It is recomputed before every substep, so the solver takes smaller steps when the field gets faster. Near the target the diffusive limit dominates.

Rule of thumb

The equation changes; the method does not. As soon as a discretisation advances the equation by one control interval, the same learning code can be applied. The actuators can be as many as needed: in a cylinder-wake experiment with eight loudspeakers, each loudspeaker forms one component of the action.

Environment 3: Kuramoto–Sivashinsky, where long waves grow

KS adds two terms to Burgers-type advection: a second derivative that destabilises and a fourth derivative that damps. On a periodic domain each Fourier mode with wavenumber κ obeys, in the linear part, dû/dt = (κ² − κ⁴) û. The sign of that growth rate decides everything.

Each growing wavenumber appears as a cosine and a sine, so ℓ = 22 gives three unstable pairs: a six-dimensional real unstable subspace around the equilibrium u = 0. The nonlinear term moves energy from the growing long waves to the damped short ones. That competition keeps the field in permanent irregular motion although the equation is deterministic.

The time integrator is ETDRK4, the fourth-order exponential time-differencing Runge–Kutta method. It integrates the stiff linear part exactly in Fourier space and treats the nonlinear term explicitly through Runge–Kutta stages. Five mean-free Gaussian actuators act on the field, and the target is the unstable equilibrium u★ = 0, so the reward penalises field energy plus 0.01·‖a‖².

In practice

A chaotic problem needs great care with the solver. An Euler method here in place of a Runge–Kutta would be impossible: the fourth derivative would force an impractically small step, and small errors grow along a chaotic trajectory.

Where episodes start, and which starts are kept for testing

For heat and Burgers every start is smooth and vanishes at both walls. For KS, small perturbations of u = 0 would be the wrong test: the controller must face developed chaos. So the KS experiment runs the uncontrolled equation through a 100-step transient onto its attractor (the set of states the system keeps visiting) and keeps the next 600 states: 400 for training, 100 for validation, 100 for testing.

Two limits are worth knowing. The three KS pools are consecutive stretches of one trajectory and touch in time; independent simulations would be stronger. And in all three experiments "unseen" means not drawn during training. The test starts still come from the same family as the training starts.

The classical reference changes with the physics

Recall from Lesson 3: the linear-quadratic regulator (LQR) is the feedback a = a★ − K(s − s★) that is optimal for a linear model with a quadratic cost, with K from the Riccati equation. The design method stays the same on all three equations. What it is worth depends on how well a linear model describes the states it is tested on.

Exact LQR (heat)The plant is linear and known, so LQR with Q = I/39 and R = 0.02 I is the optimum of this cost, apart from the clipping of actions. Learning is not expected to beat it.
Local LQR (Burgers)No single linear model is exact. The Jacobians of the one-interval map are estimated around (s★, a★) by centred differences, ε = 10⁻⁴. Stable near the target; it can degrade far from it.
Reduced local LQR (KS)Linearise at u = 0, project on the cosine and sine of modes 1 to 3, compute the gain there, and leave the short waves to their own damping. Optimal for the reduced linear dynamics only.

In every case Q and R mirror the reward weights, so the learner and the classical controller optimise the same balance of tracking and effort on the same bounded actuators. That is what makes the comparison fair.

Results: how training went

On heat and Burgers the curve falls at every check and is still falling at update 80 in all three runs, so the "best" actor is simply the last one. On KS the same code moves up and down, and the best actor came at update 85 in run B, and at 65 and 70 in the other two. Here keeping the best validated actor does real work.

In practice

On Burgers the curve was still going slowly toward better results, so training stopped too early. Instead of 80 updates, about 200 would be the first thing to try, then more layers or longer training.

One more thing to watch is the exploration noise σ. It barely moved in any of the three runs (0.368 to about 0.361 for heat and Burgers, near 0.495 throughout for KS), which says the policies never committed sharply.

Results: learned controller against the classical reference

Mean test costDo nothingLQRActor–critic, run Arun Brun C
Heat, 30 fields1.0070.3790.4350.4370.443
Burgers, 30 fields0.5990.262 (local)0.3120.3070.300
KS, 20 states114.3275.5 (local)107.8103.4109.7
KS, 240 steps, one test state377.5805.5312.9298.6not run
KS, final energy after 240 steps0.8482.670.6530.604not run

The finding is best stated in terms of cost. Measured against a classical controller on the same unseen cases, the learned controller's cost stays above the classical one where the classical design is exact (heat, +15.5 %) or locally valid (Burgers, +17.2 %). It falls below it only on the chaotic equation (KS, −62.5 %), where that design is applied far from the state it was designed for. Since lower cost is better, LQR wins on heat and Burgers and loses on KS.

Read the KS win with care. The local LQR is designed for small deviations from u = 0 and tested on chaotic states; there it costs 2.41 times as much as no control, and on one recorded state its actions sat at the bound in 97.5 % of the values. The actor–critic's gain over no control is modest: 9.6 %, 5.7 % and 4.0 % in runs B, A and C, while two runs with the same seeds differed by 6.34 in mean cost. Over 240 steps, three times the training horizon, the field under every controller was still moving irregularly. Nobody stabilised u = 0.

On heat and Burgers the learned controller still removes about half of the do-nothing cost (56.6 % and 48.7 %). What keeps it above LQR is visible in the recorded rollouts: its actions settle slightly off the holding action, at (0.564, 0.365) against a★ = (0.55, 0.35) on heat, which leaves a small steady offset that LQR does not have.

Key idea

The classical controller is a reference, and its worth depends on where it is used. Where its model is valid it is the benchmark to match. Where it is used outside its design range, beating it says little about learning. The comparison that matters on KS is against no control, and that gain is of the same order as the run-to-run difference.

How to judge a learned controller

A single good trajectory proves little, and for a chaotic system nothing, because trajectories separate quickly whatever the controller does. A rule of thumb: never trust a single rollout; use 50 to 80 starts, the deterministic policy, report means, spread and failure rates, and extend the horizon when the target is unstable. The three PDE experiments here use 30, 30 and 20 starts, which is on the low side for rankings this close.

The "±" in such results is the spread over starting states. It is not an uncertainty of the mean, and it says nothing about how much a second training run would differ. Each learned number above is one training run; only several seeds would measure that variability.

Common questions

Can early stopping be used when training a controller?

Yes, in an adapted form. There is no fixed dataset to overfit, so the budget is expressed in episodes. The actor–critic experiments add the validation part: every five updates the deterministic actor is scored on fixed validation starts, and the best actor is restored at the end.

Would a finer grid change the heat-equation results?

Not really. The 41-point grid already solves this smooth linear problem with a very small error. Refinement matters for Burgers at lower viscosity, where a stable calculation can still be too diffusive to resolve a steep front.

Why a fourth-order Runge–Kutta scheme for KS instead of Euler?

The equation is chaotic and stiff. Small errors grow along the trajectory, and the fourth derivative would force an explicit Euler step to be impractically small. ETDRK4 integrates the stiff linear part exactly in Fourier space and treats the nonlinear term to fourth order.

What if only a few sensors are available, as in an experiment?

That is the realistic case. One observation then no longer determines the next state, so the problem stops being Markov for the observer. A recurrent policy that uses the observation history is the natural extension; a variation worth trying restricts the observation, for instance to five temperatures.

Connect the dots

The thread through the whole lesson is one interface. Nothing in the learner reads the matrices or the solver; it only calls step. That is why the physics could be exchanged three times while the code stayed, and also why every exchange needs retraining: the policy is tuned to the transitions it saw.

  • A PDE becomes an environment once it can be advanced by one control interval. An unstable or biased solver teaches the wrong control problem.
  • Choose the equilibrium action first and derive a reachable target from it. Penalise the deviation from that action.
  • Anatomy: the actor fills the Policy slot and the critic the slot that was empty until now; both read the whole field, and only the actor’s output leaves the agent. One update moves 6,785 + 6,850 + 2 weights from two single-number losses.
  • Actor–critic replaces the return by the advantage over a learned value. Batches of episodes, a Huber critic loss, gradient clipping and validation-based selection keep training stable.
  • LQR has the lower cost on the linear heat equation, and local LQR edges out the actor–critic on Burgers. On chaotic KS the local LQR is worse than no control and the actor–critic lowers the energy only slightly.
  • Never trust a single rollout.

Check yourself

If the critic predicted every return exactly, what would the advantages be, and what would the actor learn from that batch?

All advantages would be zero, so the actor's gradient from the policy term would vanish: nothing in the batch turned out better or worse than expected. The actor only moves when outcomes differ from the critic's expectation.

Why does an update use eight episodes instead of one?

One trajectory describes one starting profile, and its return is dominated by that start. Eight episodes from eight random starts give 960 steps, so the gradient estimate is more representative. This lowers the noise in addition to what the critic's baseline removes.

Between the heat experiment and the Burgers experiment, which parts of the code change and which stay?

The environment step changes (a Rusanov-flux Burgers solver with adaptive substeps in place of A s + B a), the target is found by integrating to a steady state, and the classical reference becomes a local LQR from a numerical linearisation. The networks, the training loop and every training setting are the same code.

Why does the KS reward penalise ‖a‖² while the heat and Burgers rewards penalise ‖a − a★‖²?

On heat and Burgers the target is held by a nonzero action a★, so effort must be measured from it; penalising a itself would reward switching off the forcing that holds the target. On KS the target u = 0 needs no forcing, so a★ = 0 and the two forms coincide.

With ℓ = 22, how many Fourier modes of KS are unstable, and why is that number six?

The growth rate κ² − κ⁴ is positive for 0 < κ < 1. The wavenumbers that fit the domain are 2πn/22 ≈ 0.286 n, so n = 1, 2, 3 grow and n = 4 (κ ≈ 1.14) decays. Each growing wavenumber has a cosine and a sine, which gives six real unstable directions.

In one update of the heat experiment, which arrays reach the critic and the actor, what shape do the two losses and the gradients have, and where does the gradient stop?

The critic receives the 960 × 39 states and the 960 returns. The actor receives the same states, the 960 × 2 raw actions it sampled and the 960 standardised advantages. Each loss is one number. Each gradient has the shape of the weights it moves: 6,785 numbers for the critic, 6,850 + 2 for the actor and log σ. The gradient stops at the network weights; the solver inside step() only produced the data and is never differentiated.

The actor–critic's cost is 62.5 % below the local LQR's on KS. Is that a success of learning?

It is not shown. The local LQR is designed at u = 0 and tested on chaotic states far from it, where it costs 2.41 times as much as no control. Against no control the learned gain is 4.0 to 9.6 % over three runs, the same order as the difference between two training runs (6.34), and no controller stabilised the equilibrium.

Which algorithm for which problem, and what changes when the KS environment is rewritten to that standard?

One line on what comes later: control of real flows, with turbulence and many agents, is Lesson 7.
