From Lesson 4

Lesson 4 ended with a hand-written actor–critic that held the chaotic Kuramoto–Sivashinsky (KS) field down where a local LQR could not. Every line of that loop was written by hand: the environment class, the two networks, the update. Research groups do not write that loop again for each problem. They pick a tested algorithm from a library and connect it to their solver through a standard interface. This lesson opens that toolbox.

A map of the algorithm families

Lesson 2 named two routes from the Bellman equations to an algorithm. A value-based method learns Q and acts greedily on it. A policy-based method adjusts the policy directly. An actor–critic does both. A second question cuts across the first: may the algorithm learn from old data?

On-policy means the algorithm learns only from data produced by the policy it has right now. Off-policy means it can also learn from transitions produced by older or different policies. The textbook pair is SARSA, which updates with the action actually taken next, and Q-learning, which updates with the best action while a different behaviour policy explores.

You have already met two boxes. REINFORCE is Lesson 3, and the batched actor–critic of Lesson 4 is the on-policy actor–critic in the middle column. The rest of the map is this lesson.

Q-learning: move an estimate toward a target

Value-based learning turns the Bellman optimality equation of Lesson 2 into an update rule. One sampled transition (s, a, r, s′) gives a target, the reward just received plus the discounted value of the best action available next. The stored estimate Q(s, a) is moved toward it.

target = r + γ · maxa′ Q(s′, a′)     then     Q(s, a) ← a step toward the target

The max is what makes it off-policy. The target asks what the best next action would be worth, whatever action the exploring agent takes next. With a table of Q values, repeated updates converge to the optimal Q. A table does not scale to large state spaces, which is the reason for the next step.

DQN: the table becomes a network, with two stabilisers

In the deep Q-network (DQN) a neural network Qω with parameters ω replaces the table. The update becomes a regression loss, the squared gap between target and estimate, averaged over stored transitions.

L(ω) = E(s,a,r,s′) ~ D [ ( r + γ · maxa′ Qω⁻(s′, a′) − Qω(s, a) )² ]

Two symbols in the loss carry the two stabilisers. D is the replay buffer, a store of past transitions from which random minibatches are drawn. Press Play and watch it fill: once full, the oldest transition is overwritten, and each minibatch mixes old and new experience. Replay is possible only because the method is off-policy.

ω⁻ are the parameters of the target network, a copy of the Q network that is updated only slowly, or only every many steps. In the animation its label counts the steps since the last copy.

Key idea

The target contains the network being trained. Change ω to reduce the gap and the target moves too, so learning chases a moving target. A frozen copy gives the network a fixed goal for a while. In CFD terms it is like lagging a coefficient: you hold it from the previous outer iteration so that the inner solve has something fixed to converge to.

Why the max breaks, and how DDPG removes it

The maximum over actions is the weak point of DQN. For a continuous, high-dimensional action, such as a blowing velocity at every wall point of a channel, it cannot be computed. Seen from the other side, DQN chooses among a finite list of actions, so it does not fit a continuous force.

The deep deterministic policy gradient (DDPG) removes the max. A deterministic actor μ(s) supplies the action. The critic is trained with the DQN loss above, with the next action taken from the actor instead of from a maximisation. The actor is moved along the gradient of the critic with respect to the action.

A deterministic actor never samples, so exploration comes from noise added to its output. DDPG is off-policy: it learns from a replay buffer filled by earlier versions of the policy, which reuses expensive simulation data. The channel-flow study of Lesson 7 uses exactly this algorithm.

TD3, the twin delayed deep deterministic policy gradient, belongs to the same off-policy, deterministic family. It has two additions, two critic networks and delayed policy updates, which reduce value overestimation and make training more stable. In the experiments of this lesson its configuration adds Gaussian action noise of standard deviation 0.1. SAC, the soft actor–critic, is the third off-policy option used in this guide; it maximises the expected reward together with the entropy of the policy, which encourages exploration.

In practice

The channel-flow implementation keeps PPO, DDPG and TD3 side by side in one Python library that talks to the Fortran solver. The choice made there fits in three terms: model-free, off-policy, actor–critic.

PPO: limit how far one update may move the policy

Proximal policy optimization (PPO) comes from the other side of the map. It is an on-policy actor–critic, like the loop of Lesson 4, with one addition. Each action in the batch gets a probability ratio χ: how much more likely the updated policy makes that action than the policy that collected the data. The objective rewards raising χ for good actions and lowering it for bad ones, but only inside a band around 1.

JCLIP(θ) = Et [ min( χt · Ât , clip(χt, 1 − ε, 1 + ε) · Ât ) ] ,    χt = πθ(at|st) / πθ,old(at|st)

Â is the critic's estimate of the advantage (Lesson 2). Read the picture with ε = 0.2, the value the authors of PPO tuned. For an action with positive advantage the term grows with χ up to 1.2 and then stays at 1.2·Â, so the update has no incentive to make the action more than 20 % more probable than before. For a negative advantage the term stays at 0.8·Â once χ falls below 0.8, so there is no incentive to push the probability below 80 % of its old value.

Key idea

On a flat part of the curve the gradient is zero. Moving further earns nothing, so the optimiser stops pushing that action and the new policy stays close to the old one. That is the meaning of "proximal". The clip acts only once the policy has moved: at χ = 1 the gradient is the same as in the advantage actor–critic of Lesson 4.

Switch to Â < 0 and look at the right side. Making a bad action more likely is never clipped, so the penalty keeps growing. The minimum in the formula always keeps the more pessimistic of the two expressions.

This is why PPO can afford something the Lesson 4 loop could not: several passes over the same batch. The training log of the Gymnasium point-mass experiment later in this lesson shows ten passes over each 1,024-step batch with a clip range of 0.2. In the last update of the KS training the log reports clip_fraction 0.358, so about a third of the samples had reached a flat part.

Three families, one loop

The three agents above look different on the page, but each one fills the same six slots of the loop from Lesson 1. Switch between the families and watch what changes inside the agent box, and what does not change at all: the environment. Click any box to read what it holds for that family, its input and output with their shapes, and the library argument that sets it.

Click a box in the loop to read what it holds for the selected family, its input and output, and the code it corresponds to.
Key idea

Off-policy adds two boxes: a replay buffer in the Memory slot and frozen copies of the networks. On-policy PPO has neither; its Memory is a rollout that lives for one update. The Policy slot fixes the kind of action: a list of Q values gives an index, a deterministic actor or a Gaussian mean gives a continuous vector. In every family the dashed arrows stay inside the agent box. The gradient reaches the network weights only; the solver is called, never differentiated.

On-policy or off-policy is a question about data

The trade-off fits in two sentences. On-policy PPO discards data after each update but is stable and has few tunable parameters, which is why most studies chose it. Off-policy DDPG and TD3 reuse old experience, which matters when every transition costs a time step of direct numerical simulation (DNS).

The KS problem gives a small version of this trade-off. Three pre-trained agents, one per algorithm, were each trained for about 100,000 environment steps on the same KS problem. With that equal budget of solver steps the off-policy agents reached a cost near 5 and PPO near 15. They also took several times longer to train on the clock.

Pitfall

This is one agent per algorithm, each with its own settings, so it is an observation and not a ranking. Changing the algorithm's name changes its whole configuration. On the airfoil of Lesson 6 the order comes out differently.

Intuition

The three library choices are two kinds of technique: PPO learns from the trajectories its current policy has just produced, while SAC and TD3 store everything and learn from the present and the past. In one TD3 run on KS the energy fell from about 1 to about 0.004. Methods that use a lot of information from the past can also hold the system well beyond the training horizon.

Which algorithm for my problem?

Two questions do most of the sorting. A finite list of actions allows the max of DQN. Continuous actions need an actor, and then the cost of one environment step decides whether discarding data is affordable. The KS training ran at about 1,900 environment steps per second, learning included, so PPO's wastefulness costs nothing there. A DNS step is a different matter.

Gymnasium: one interface between physics and learner

Gymnasium continues the Gym toolkit that OpenAI created. An environment is a class derived from gym.Env that declares two spaces and implements two methods, and nothing else is needed for an agent to train on it. The spaces fix shapes and bounds. Every environment in this guide uses spaces.Box, a bounded continuous vector: an action in [−1, 1] that the environment maps to a physical amplitude, and an observation whose length is the number of observed quantities.

Intuition

Gymnasium is to control what Keras is to networks. You take care of what goes in and what comes out, and the library takes care of the rest.

The plain Python classes of Lessons 1 to 4 already followed this convention by hand. Gymnasium makes it formal, and check_env tests a class against it. Here is the KS environment of this lesson, shortened; the solver call ks_step is the ETDRK4 code recalled from Lesson 4.

class KSGymEnv(gym.Env):
    def __init__(self, initial_pool, horizon=80, effort_weight=0.01):
        super().__init__()
        ...
        self.action_space = spaces.Box(low=-1.0, high=1.0, shape=(n_action,), dtype=np.float32)
        self.observation_space = spaces.Box(low=-10.0, high=10.0, shape=(n_x,), dtype=np.float32)

    def _get_obs(self):                       # scale, then clip
        return np.clip(self.state / STATE_SCALE, -10.0, 10.0).astype(np.float32)

    def reset(self, seed=None, options=None):
        super().reset(seed=seed)              # seeds self.np_random
        self.step_count = 0
        if options is not None and "initial" in options:
            self.state = np.asarray(options["initial"], dtype=np.float32).copy()
        else:                                 # a random state from the chaotic attractor
            index = self.np_random.integers(len(self.initial_pool))
            self.state = self.initial_pool[index].copy()
        return self._get_obs(), {}

    def step(self, action):
        action = np.clip(np.asarray(action, dtype=np.float32), -1.0, 1.0)
        self.state = ks_step(self.state, action)          # one control interval
        self.step_count += 1
        state_cost = np.mean(self.state**2)
        effort_cost = self.effort_weight * np.sum(action**2)
        reward = -(state_cost + effort_cost)
        terminated = False                                # no physical end
        truncated = self.step_count >= self.horizon       # time budget
        info = {"state_cost": float(state_cost), "effort_cost": float(effort_cost),
                "energy": float(0.5 * np.mean(self.state**2))}
        return self._get_obs(), float(reward), terminated, truncated, info

Two details are worth copying. reset accepts a prescribed start through options, which the evaluation uses so that every controller is tested from exactly the same states. And the observation is normalised inside the environment, by a scale computed from the training pool only, so the network always works with numbers of order one.

Training with Stable-Baselines3 in a few lines

training_env = Monitor(KSGymEnv(training_pool, horizon=80, effort_weight=0.01),
                       filename=str(SAVE_DIR / "monitor.csv"))

model = PPO(policy="MlpPolicy", env=training_env, learning_rate=3e-4, n_steps=1024,
            batch_size=64, gamma=0.99, policy_kwargs=dict(net_arch=[96, 96]),
            verbose=1, seed=SEED)

model.learn(total_timesteps=100_000)
model.save(FINAL_MODEL)

def drl_controller(state):
    obs = np.clip(np.asarray(state, dtype=np.float32) / STATE_SCALE, -10.0, 10.0)
    action, _ = model.predict(obs, deterministic=True)
    return np.asarray(action, dtype=np.float32)

Monitor is a wrapper: it passes every call through to the environment and records the return and length of each episode. The library adds one more wrapper by itself, a vectorised environment (the log prints "Wrapping the env in a DummyVecEnv"). "MlpPolicy" builds the actor and the critic as multilayer perceptrons, here with two hidden layers of 96 neurons. predict(..., deterministic=True) switches the exploration off, so the same state always gives the same action, as with PD and LQR.

What learn does with those 100,000 steps, one update at a time, with the array shapes of the KS experiment. Press Step to follow one update from the solver calls to the new weights.

Press Step to walk through the six stages of one update with the numbers of the KS training run.
The library does
  • the actor and critic networks
  • collecting rollouts or filling the replay buffer
  • the update rule (clipping, target networks, noise)
  • logging, saving and loading
You still own
  • the environment: physics, time step, actuators, bounds
  • the observation and its scaling
  • the reward and the horizon
  • the evaluation: unseen starts, classical references, seeds

The two lists drawn onto the loop. Every slot on the environment side is a method or an attribute you write; every slot on the agent side is built by the library from the two spaces it finds on the environment. Click a slot for the code it corresponds to.

Click a slot to see who owns it and the code it corresponds to.

To train SAC or TD3 instead, one string changes. That string brings a configuration with it: SAC and TD3 with a buffer of 100,000 transitions and batches of 256, TD3 with a learning rate of 1e-3 on KS and action noise 0.1. A caution from practice: a standard library is convenient but not always the right tool for a real simulation, where the loop may have to be written by hand.

Rule of thumb

Fix the random seeds of NumPy, the network library and the environment while you develop and debug, so that a change in behaviour can be traced to a change in the code. Remove them only when you trust the code.

The Gymnasium point-mass experiment: the same plant through the library

The Gymnasium point-mass experiment takes the point mass of Lesson 3 and changes one thing: the class becomes a Gymnasium environment and PPO from the library does the learning. Dynamics, reward, horizon, PD gains, LQR weights and the 50 test starts are identical, and the PD and LQR costs reproduce those of Lesson 3 to every printed digit.

The exact statement is that PPO and the optimal linear controller ended level. PPO's mean cost is lower by 0.104, while each mean spreads by about 32 over the 50 starts. A second training run with the same seed gave the identical number, which shows that the run is reproducible and says nothing about how much it would vary with another seed. For comparison, the hand-written REINFORCE of Lesson 3 scored 483.60 on the same starts.

Training took 50,176 steps, 49 rollouts of 1,024, which is about 627 episodes and 12 seconds on a CPU. In the log the mean episode return rose from −252 to −30 and the exploration spread σ fell from 0.985 to 0.82. On a known linear plant nobody needs a learned controller. The value of the experiment is that the same interface carries over to problems where no such model exists.

The Gymnasium KS experiment: suppressing chaos with PPO

Lesson 4 recap in two lines: the KS equation has a destabilising second derivative, a damping fourth derivative and a nonlinear term, and on a periodic domain of length 22 six Fourier modes are unstable, which makes the field chaotic. The target u = 0 is a solution but an unstable one, so the controller has to keep working to hold it.

ObservationThe full field on 64 points, divided by the standard deviation of the training states and clipped to ±10.Box(64)
ActionFive actuator amplitudes, each held for one control interval of 4 solver steps.Box(5) in [−1, 1]
RewardMinus the mean squared field and a small charge for actuation.r = −[mean(u²) + 0.01·Σa²]
EpisodeStarts from a stored chaotic state (400 for training, 100 validation, 100 test) and is truncated after 80 decisions.γ = 0.99
Intuition

The horizon is not a physical time. It is how many steps ahead you let the consequences of an action show, and γ decides how much the late ones still count: 0.9980 is about 0.45, while 0.980 is almost zero. A long horizon sees further and makes every episode cost more, which becomes prohibitive when a step is a CFD run.

The local LQR is designed on the six unstable Fourier modes around u = 0, and its reduced closed loop is stable (spectral radius 0.814). It still fails, because episodes start on the chaotic attractor, far from the point where the linear model holds, and its saturated commands push the field away. PPO was trained from those states. During training the policy beat the uncontrolled run after 2,000 steps but needed 88,000 to bring a validation state below 5 % of the chaotic energy, and only 5.2 % of its final commands sit at the ±1 bound.

Pitfall

A learned result is one sample. The run shown here gave a PPO cost of 14.63; the same code and seed on another machine gave 21.77. The solver, the LQR and the uncontrolled runs agree to every printed digit. Quote learned numbers with their run.

Full write-up

This experiment is Stage 1 of the airfoil project, with all its exercises, the regulator and model-predictive references, and the numbers behind them: a flap controller trained inside a CFD-built surrogate, Stage 1.

Eight variations: where the result stops holding

Eight variations of the Gymnasium KS experiment change one ingredient at a time. Each retrained agent is PPO with the main settings, 100,000 steps, one seed, so differences of a few percent are noise. "Success" means a final energy below 5 % of the mean uncontrolled energy, and "returned to chaos" means above 50 % of it.

More unstable modes means a harder problem. At ℓ = 12 there is no chaos, everything is essentially linear and LQR can do the job; at ℓ = 30 things are more chaotic and harder to control.

VariationWhat was changedWhat the numbers show
Threshold rewardNo penalty once the field is below 10 % of its typical mean squareIt did not reduce the control effort (5.64 against 5.18 over 240 steps) and the field spent less time under the threshold (48 % against 76 %).
One actuator failsOne output forced to zero after training, 240 stepsCost 32 to 70 against 34.7 with all five. Losing actuator 1 (64.1) or 4 (70.0) hurts most. A return to chaos appeared in 2 % of the cases, for actuator 4 only.
Lyapunov sensitivityTwo runs started 10⁻⁴ apartGrowth rate 0.072 without control, 0.122 with LQR, 0.034 with PPO. Separation after 240 steps: 11.0, 13.6 and 0.08.
Key idea

None of these limits is about the algorithm. Too few actuators, too few sensors, a reward that does not say what you want, a system that differs from the training one: these belong to the environment, which is the part you own. The Lyapunov sensitivity test adds a subtler point. Two controlled trajectories may still drift apart; the objective is a low energy, and that can hold even when individual trajectories diverge.

Connect the dots

The algorithms differ in what they learn and in which data they may use. The interface hides which physics produces the transitions. Put together, the choice of learner and the choice of model become two separate decisions, and the evidence from the experiments says the second one deserves most of the attention: what is observed, what is actuated, what is rewarded, and how much each step costs.

Check yourself

Why can DQN not control the five KS actuators directly?

Its target needs the maximum of Q over all actions. With a finite list that is a comparison. With five continuous amplitudes there is no list to scan, so the maximum cannot be computed. DDPG, TD3 and SAC put an actor in its place, and PPO optimises the policy directly.

What problem does the target network solve, and what would you see without it?

The target r + γ max Q is computed by the network that is being trained, so each update also moves the target. A copy that is refreshed only slowly holds the target still between copies. Without it the estimate keeps chasing a goal that shifts at every step.

In the PPO picture with ε = 0.2 and Â > 0, the ratio of some action has reached 1.35. What does this sample contribute to the next gradient step?

Nothing. Beyond χ = 1.2 the term stays at 1.2·Â, so its slope is zero. The update has no incentive to make that action even more probable, which keeps the new policy close to the old one.

Each environment step is one DNS time step of a turbulent channel. Which family do you try first, and what do you pay for it?

An off-policy actor–critic such as DDPG or TD3, because every stored transition is reused in many updates instead of being discarded after one. The price is a replay buffer and a configuration of its own to tune, where PPO is known for stability and few settings.

An environment returns terminated = False at every step and truncated = True at step 80. What does that tell the algorithm?

That the episode stopped because the time budget ran out and the physics did not end. All environments in this guide behave this way, since none has a physical end state.

With five point sensors the KS policy costs 98.3, with the full field 14.6. Why does stacking the last four observations help, and why only partly?

One snapshot of five values does not determine the state of the field, so the same observation can call for different actions. Several past snapshots carry some of the missing information, such as how the pattern is moving. The cost falls to 69.4, still far from 14.6, because four frames of five points do not replace 64 points.

In the loop with the three families, switch from PPO to TD3. Which slots change and which stay the same?

Only the agent box changes. The Memory slot turns from a rollout of 1,024 steps that is used once into a replay buffer of 100,000 transitions sampled 256 at a time, a box with target copies of the actor and the critic appears, exploration becomes noise added to a deterministic action instead of sampling from a learned σ, and the critic takes the action as an input. The environment, its spaces, reset, step and reward are untouched: the library sizes the new networks from the same two spaces.

Into Lesson 6

The KS agent needed 100,352 environment steps, and the solver delivered them in about a minute. One action on a two-dimensional OpenFOAM airfoil takes about a minute of computing. The same number of steps would then be about 70 days of solver time, for a single training run with a single seed. Lesson 6 asks what to train on instead: a zero-dimensional airfoil model first, then a network that has learned lift and drag from CFD data.

Lesson 6 of 7 · 0-D airfoil model · RANS surrogate · surrogate in the loop · field model (POD / β-VAE)

Airfoil control: reduced models and CFD surrogates

What to put inside the environment when the real simulator is too slow to train on. After this lesson you can draw the ladder of models from a three-equation airfoil to full CFD, explain how a surrogate is built, validated and plugged into the loop, and say where it can fool the agent.

From Lesson 5

Lesson 5 ended with library algorithms (PPO, SAC, TD3 from Stable-Baselines3) training on any Gymnasium environment, and with one uncomfortable number: training takes tens of thousands of environment steps. So far each step was a cheap ordinary or partial differential equation. This lesson asks what happens when each step is a CFD run.

What if every step is a CFD run?

The multiplication is the whole argument: steps needed × cost per step. The agent cannot learn from fewer steps just because the solver is expensive. Serial CFD at a minute per step would take about five weeks for the 50,000-step budget; even an optimistic estimate for the job is one to two weeks. With a model call that takes about 0.01 ms, the aerodynamics disappear from the bill and all the remaining time is the learning itself.

In practice

Every time the agent moves the flap, the simulation has to be advanced to see the consequence. With OpenFOAM, even in 2D, that is about a minute per interaction, so calibrating the flap agent may take one or two weeks, and in 3D the cost is out of reach. The way out: build a second neural network that already knows the aerodynamics, and let the agent train against that.

The fidelity ladder

Each step up answers a weakness of the one below. The analytic model knows only a straight lift line. The coefficient surrogate knows camber, thickness, Reynolds number and the bend of the lift curve, because it was fitted to RANS results. The field model carries the same information through a compressed picture of the whole flow, so it can also show pressure and velocity. Full CFD is the only step with the actual moving flap and unsteady flow, and it is too slow to sit in the loop.

Key idea

The reinforcement-learning formulation (observation, action, reward, reset, step) and the aerodynamic model are two separate things. The ladder changes only the second. The learned policy still depends on which step produced its training experience.

The control problem: hold the lift through a gust

This is a disturbance-rejection problem. Nothing has to be driven to a new place, as in the point mass of Lesson 1. The lift already sits at its target and the task is to keep it there while a gust passes. The model is a toy on purpose: it is cheap to train on and it is formulated exactly as a CFD-based environment would be.

The 0-D model: one static law and two lags

αeff = α0 + αgust + kf·δf     CL,qs = 2π·αeff  (radians)
τL·dCL/dt = CL,qs − CL     τf·dδf/dt = δf,cmd − δf
CD = CD0 + kD·CL2 + kδ·δf2     with CD0 = 0.012, kD = 0.025, kδ = 0.08
wg(t) = (W0/2)·[1 − cos(2π·(t − t0)/Tg)] for t0 ≤ t ≤ t0 + Tg, else 0
αgust = atan(wg/U∞)

The first line is thin-airfoil theory with the flap folded in as an extra angle. The second line is a pair of first-order lags, the same form as a relaxation toward a steady state in a solver. Training draws a new gust for every episode: amplitude W0 from −3 to 3 m/s, duration Tg from 0.8 to 1.8 s, start t0 from 1 to 3 s.

# inside step(): explicit Euler, dt = 0.05 s
self.flap_deg += (self.dt / self.tau_flap) * (flap_command_deg - self.flap_deg)
cl_qs, cd, alpha_eff_deg = self._aero(gust_angle_deg)   # the only aerodynamic call
self.cl += (self.dt / self.tau_lift) * (cl_qs - self.cl)

There is no mesh and no spatial coordinate, which is what "0-D" means here. Since the numerics cost nothing, if training takes time, it is the machine learning and nothing else. The environment also offers a saturating law, CL,max·tanh(2πα / CL,max) with CL,max = 1.35, because the straight line grows without limit. It still is no stall model.

The same problem as observation, action and reward

Every observation is divided by a typical size (1.5, 1.5, 10° and the 20° flap limit) so that all four inputs are of order one. The rule: scale every observation and every reward term to order one, or the largest quantity dominates and the agent optimises that one alone. An episode is 120 steps of 0.05 s, six seconds of flight, and the discount factor is γ = 0.99.

The gust angle in the observation matters. With it the agent can act the moment the gust arrives (feedforward). Without it the agent can only react after the lift has already moved (feedback). One of the variations below removes it.

Feel it: fly the gust yourself

Below is the 0-D model environment running in this page with the same equations and constants as the training experiment (linear lift law, evaluation gust W0 = 2.5 m/s, Tg = 1.3 s, starting at 2 s, explicit Euler with 0.05 s). Move the flap slider to see the steady lift change. Then fly the gust by hand, or let one of two hand-written rules try.

Two things are worth trying. First the proportional rule, a = −K·(CL − target): it only moves after an error exists, so the error never fully vanishes and raising K helps. Then the gust-cancelling rule, δcmd = −αgust / kf: it uses the measured gust, moves at once, and is limited only by the flap lag. The −1/kf = −1.82 in that rule is the ratio the trained agent is compared against below.

In practice

The trained agent is not compared with a classical controller here. It is not difficult to add an LQR, and if the problem is linear a classical controller will be better. The experiment is there to show that a model can simplify the problem drastically and that a learning method captures the behaviour of the system. The learning method earns its place when the problem is nonlinear.

The simulation above agrees with that. On this linear model the gust-cancelling rule scores about the same as the trained TD3 agent, and the proportional rule gets there with a high gain. That is an observation from this page's illustration, with rules that know the model's constants; it is not a tuned classical baseline.

Training on the 0-D model, and what the agent learned

The error drops six to thirteen times depending on the gust, with a mean flap deflection of about 1° and a peak of 8° on the evaluation gust. The flap starts to move at the gust onset (t = 2.10 s), before the uncontrolled lift error exceeds 0.01 (t = 2.20 s): the agent uses the observed gust angle to anticipate. At the gust peak the flap has moved −7.82° against a gust angle of +4.76°, a ratio of −1.64 where pure cancellation needs −1.82.

Pitfall: one seed is one sample

A PPO agent trained on the same environment reaches a controlled RMSE of 0.0074 on the evaluation gust; the TD3 agent shown here gives 0.0166. The uncontrolled value, 0.1385, is identical in both. Each number comes from one training run with one seed. Treat differences of this size between single training runs as noise until several seeds agree.

Full write-up

The 0-D model experiment is Stage 2 of the airfoil project: Stages 1 and 2 of the project page.

Seven what-ifs on the cheap model

Because one training run costs seconds to minutes, every what-if question can be answered with an experiment. Each bar is a newly trained agent (TD3 unless stated, 50,000 steps, one seed).

Hiding the gust angle is the partial-observability test. Hiding the gust angle turns the agent into a pure feedback controller, and in this run it lost nothing: the measured lift carried enough information for these gusts. The smoothness and drag variations show the reward doing its job. Without the smoothness term the commands get rougher and the error does not improve; with a fifty times heavier drag weight the agent buys a slightly lower drag with a larger lift error.

These three are the first sight of the theme that runs through the rest of the lesson. A policy is only tested where it was trained. Change the actuator (the slower flap) or the size of the disturbance (the stronger gusts) and the error grows about three times, although the algorithm and the network are untouched. Retraining on the new condition repairs it. The saturating lift law is a change the linear-trained policy tolerates, because for these gusts the two laws stay close.

Step 2 of the ladder: building a surrogate from RANS data

AirfRANS holds incompressible two-dimensional RANS solutions of NACA four- and five-digit airfoils for Reynolds numbers from 2 to 6 million and angles of attack from −5° to 15°. The experiment keeps the four-digit family, whose shape is three numbers: maximum camber m, its position p and thickness t (2, 4, 12 for a NACA 2412-like section). AirfRANS samples them continuously, so the 489 cases are 489 different shapes and conditions.

The output scaling is the step people skip. CL spans about −0.5 to 1.9 and CD about 0.007 to 0.035, so a mean squared error on raw values would see only the lift. Standardising each target separately, with scalers fitted on the training set only, puts both on the same footing in the loss. Training stopped after 364 epochs and restored the weights of epoch 324, the best validation loss.

Pitfall: drag comes first

The force-coefficient method of the AirfRANS Simulation class returns drag first and lift second. Swap them and the surrogate trains without complaint on the wrong targets.

How good is the surrogate, and where?

On the 111 test casesCL RMSECL R²CD RMSECD R²
Surrogate, run A (the one used in the loop below)0.02590.99790.000870.9724
Surrogate, run B (retrained, same code and seed)0.02090.99860.001000.9632
Thin-airfoil theory 2πα0.3595

On unseen cases inside the database the surrogate is about 14 times more accurate in lift than thin-airfoil theory. Drag is harder: it is small and sensitive to pressure and viscous details, and in a parity plot one test case sits clearly off the diagonal. All of this is an interpolation score. The test cases lie inside the cloud of training cases, which is checked by plotting the parameter space before fitting anything.

Data. With 38 cases the lift error is 0.19, eight times the full-data value; from 189 cases on the curve flattens. The CFD budget of a surrogate is a design decision with a measurable return. Range. A network trained only inside a band of Reynolds number or angle makes two to five times larger errors outside it, with the same architecture and settings. Size. The smallest network wins on 378 cases. Inputs. Dropping the Reynolds number costs little in lift and clearly more in drag, which is partly viscous.

Ensemble. Five networks trained from different seeds, averaged, halve the lift error (0.0129 against 0.0245 for one member). Their disagreement, the spread, doubles outside the training angles, so it works as a cheap warning light for extrapolation. It is a rough one: the spread correlates with the actual drag error (rank correlation 0.53) and hardly with the lift error (0.11).

What the surrogate cannot do

It is static: it returns steady RANS coefficients and knows nothing of unsteady lift, vortex shedding, dynamic stall or gust history. It has no flap input, because AirfRANS contains no deflected flaps. And outside the ranges of its database it returns smooth, plausible numbers with no warning attached.

Plugging the model into the loop: swap one box

The surrogate-in-the-loop airfoil experiment takes the environment of the 0-D model and replaces the function _aero. The result is a loop with two neural networks in it, and they play opposite roles. Click any component to see what it holds, what goes in and out, and the code it corresponds to.

Two networks, two roles. The policy network is the thing being trained: its weights change after every step of the 50,000. The surrogate network is part of the physics: it was fitted once to RANS data, it is called 50,000 times, and its weights never move. Nothing in the agent knows or cares that the plant contains a network. Press the buttons below to exchange the aerodynamic model and watch what else moves.

Agent sideObservation (4 scaled numbers), action, reward terms and weights, γ = 0.99, 120-step episodes, 50,000 training stepsThe main run uses SAC (the 0-D model run used TD3)
DynamicsFlap lag 0.10 s, lift lag 0.18 s, gust shape and ranges, flap effectiveness 0.55Nothing
AerodynamicsThe flap still enters only as an equivalent angleCL,qs and CD come from the surrogate; Re and (m, p, t) become environment parameters; the target becomes the surrogate's zero-gust lift, 0.7595 (the 0-D model used 0.55)
Key idea

Replacing 2πα by the surrogate changes the map from (state, action) to (next state, reward). So the best policy can change although observation, action, reward weights and algorithm are identical. Put plainly: a DRL controller can only be as trustworthy as the environment used to train and validate it.

It helps to be exact about what this is: steady CFD-informed coefficients embedded in low-order unsteady dynamics, and no CFD simulation of a moving flap. A flap-dependent, ideally unsteady, dataset would remove the equivalent-angle shortcut. Such data are hard to find.

Two networks, two kinds of learning

Open both boxes. On the left, the networks of the agent: the actor that turns four observation numbers into one flap command, and the critics that score a state and an action. On the right, the surrogate inside the plant. Same building blocks, opposite roles.

The two networks were also trained in different ways, and the picture below puts the two procedures side by side. The surrogate learned by supervised regression: every input row has a known answer from RANS, the loss is a distance to that answer, and a few hundred passes over 378 rows are enough. The policy learned by reinforcement: nobody knows the right flap command, the loss is built from rewards and the critic's own estimate, and the data are generated while learning. Press Step to walk through the stages in parallel.

Key idea

Gradients flow from a loss into the weights of the network that owns the loss, and nowhere else. The surrogate's gradients stopped when its fit ended. During reinforcement learning the surrogate, the lags and the gust are only called, never differentiated: the agent learns from the rewards they return, exactly as it would from a CFD solver.

What the surrogate environment taught the agent

The SAC agent of the main run cuts the lift error on the evaluation gust from 0.1354 to 0.0596. That is a weaker result than with the 0-D model, and the dashboard shows why. At the gust onset the flap jumps to +9.6°, which pushes the lift up to 0.96, before it reverses to −6.5°. The same transient appeared in a repeat run with a retrained surrogate, so it belongs to this SAC training run and not to one surrogate. Its best snapshot was at step 3,000 (RMSE 0.029), and later training did not keep that level.

Train on one model, test on another

The two static laws differ by about 0.2 in lift at every angle up to 10°, and the two environments aim at different targets (0.7595 and 0.5483). An agent that never observes which model it is in cannot correct for that. A caution is in order: these are single SAC seeds, and SAC was the weakest algorithm at this budget, so the size of the asymmetry is uncertain. The direction of the lesson is not.

Change Reynolds number or the section shape

Randomising a parameter during training (domain randomisation) is the standard way to make one policy cover a family of conditions. Here it did not pay: the error rose from 0.053 to 0.089. A repeat run with a retrained surrogate showed the opposite ordering. With one seed per case, neither direction is a finding. What the experiment does establish is the procedure: draw Re in reset(), set the target to that Re's own zero-gust lift, and evaluate over the whole range.

Shape matters far more than Reynolds number. The policy carries over to sections whose lift at 5° is near the one it trained on (2418, 4412, 4415). On the symmetric 0012 and 0018 and on the strongly cambered 6409 and 6412 it does harm. Being able to test on any geometry, because geometry is a surrogate input, is different from being robust to it: nothing in the observation tells the agent which section it is flying.

Full write-up

The surrogate and the controller trained inside it, with every exercise, the domain-penalty test and the comparison of two executions, are Stages 3 and 4 of a flap controller trained inside a CFD-built surrogate.

The danger zone: where the agent takes the surrogate

The green band is the only region where anybody has checked the surrogate against CFD. The agent decides where the surrogate is evaluated, through αeq. A well-trained policy keeps αeq close to 5°, since holding the lift means cancelling the gust (PPO stays between 4.6° and 5.5°). But the flap alone can move αeq by ±11°, and an exploring agent uses that freedom. With wide gusts the unprotected SAC agent reached 19.9°, five degrees beyond any training case.

Outside the band each model continues its curve in its own way, and no CFD says which is right. Real airfoils stall there. An agent that maximises reward does not care whether a favourable lift value is physics or fitting error, which is how a policy ends up exploiting the model instead of the flow.

Pitfall: the agent exploits model error

A DRL agent searches for whatever maximises its reward, including the errors of the model it trains on. In a surrogate environment, watch where the agent drives the surrogate's inputs and penalise excursions outside the data range.

rdomain = −λdomain·[ max(0, αeq − αmax)2 + max(0, αmin − αeq)2 ]
with λdomain = 0.1 per deg², αmin = −4.91°, αmax = 14.84°

That is the protection a domain penalty adds to the reward, with the limits read from the training table instead of chosen by hand. With gusts up to ±6 m/s in training it cut the time outside the data from 4.6 % to 0.8 % and also lowered the error (0.213 against 0.261). Keep the scale in mind: on these very strong test gusts neither agent does much better than a fixed flap (0.264). The other protections: monitor αeq in every evaluation, use the spread of an ensemble as a warning, randomise the parameters the policy should be robust to, and finally test the controller on a model that was not used in training.

Step 3 of the ladder: a field model in the same environment

The field-model (POD / β-VAE) experiment builds a second route from the same 489 cases to the same two coefficients. It first compresses each whole flow field into 8 numbers, a reduced-order model (ROM), and then predicts those 8 numbers from the parameters.

On the 111 test cases the β-VAE chain predicts the coefficients about as well as the direct network (CL RMSE 0.0212 against 0.0259, CD 0.00074 against 0.00087). Most of its field error comes from the compression to 8 numbers, hardly any from predicting those numbers. For the environment, the consequences are four.

Policies transfer both ways. Compare this table with the earlier cross-test between the surrogate and the thin-airfoil model. There the two models disagreed by about 0.2 in lift and the transfer failed. Here they disagree by at most 0.05 inside the data, their targets are 0.7595 and 0.7483, and a policy trained in either environment scores the same in both. Transfer between models is as good as the agreement between the models along the path the policy flies. The cost is the same. One call takes 0.014 ms against 0.011 ms, and a PPO run takes 11 s in either environment.

It can show the flow. The three panels look almost alike, and that is the result: at the gust peak the gust adds 4.76° and the flap takes 8.25° × 0.55 away, so αeq moves only from 5.03° to 5.16°. The controller holds the flow state nearly constant. It shares the same limits. Both models saw the same 378 cases, so their trusted box is identical. The picture has no flap and no unsteadiness, because the data have none.

Full write-up

The field model, its design search and the cross-test in this environment are Part 2 of the airfoil series: reduced-order models, a β-VAE and a latent-space design search.

Is this transfer learning?

Can the simple model be used for initial training before switching to CFD? Yes: that is the purpose of the surrogate. The complete version goes through a latent space: compress many simulations with a reduced-order model, advance the latent state in time (for example with a Koopman operator), and control the latent state instead of the CFD. With about ten numbers and a decoder, that is fast.

Is that essentially transfer learning? Not quite. Transfer learning takes a model trained for one case and uses the same network for another. A latent space is trained once on simulations that vary everything of interest, and new situations come from changing the latent values. One network trained on many configurations and steered to new ones is the idea behind a foundation model. The field-model chain of this lesson is a small, static version of that idea; the time evolution in latent space is the part this lesson does not build.

In practice

Optimising lift or drag with a surrogate is easy, because it is optimising one function. Then validate with CFD, which takes only one CFD simulation.

The working rule: train cheap, test on something better, know your range

The cheap model is where the thousands of trials happen. The better model is the examiner, and it must be one the agent did not train on. The range check says whether the examiner's own answers can be trusted along the path the policy takes. The same pattern appears at research scale: agents trained only on a cheap channel-flow environment that were then applied to a wing section without retraining.

Connect the dots

Read the map from the top row to the bottom row. The top row is what you build: a ladder of models, an environment that does not care which one it holds, and a recipe for turning CFD data into a fast function. The bottom row is what you owe the result: knowing how it fails, guarding against that, and seeing where the idea is heading.

Check yourself

Why can't the flap agent simply be trained on OpenFOAM?

Training needs tens of thousands of environment steps, 50,000 in the experiments of this lesson, and each step must advance the flow. At about one minute per interaction that is on the order of 35 days of solver time for one training run, against under a second of model calls with the surrogate.

In going from the 0-D model to the surrogate in the loop, which lines of the environment change, and why can the learned policy still be different?

Only the aerodynamic function _aero (and with it the zero-gust target, 0.7595 in place of 0.55). Observation, action, reward weights, lags, gust and algorithm settings stay. The policy can differ because the map from state and action to next state and reward is different, and the policy is optimal only for the transitions it trained on.

The surrogate has no flap input. How does the flap act with the surrogate in the loop, and what does that cost in realism?

Through an equivalent angle, αeq = α₀ + αgust + 0.55·δf, at which the steady surrogate is evaluated; the flap lag and the lift lag supply the dynamics. So the environment is steady RANS coefficients inside low-order dynamics. It contains no flow around a deflected flap and no unsteady aerodynamics.

The surrogate scores R² = 0.998 for lift on the test set. Why is that no licence to use it at α = 18°?

The test cases lie inside the training cloud, so the score measures interpolation. The data end at 14.84°. At 18° the three models fitted to the same cases give 1.83, 1.73 and 1.69, none shows stall, and nothing in the output warns about it. The training-band variation measured the same effect: errors two to five times larger outside a training band.

The surrogate / thin-airfoil cross-test and the surrogate / field-model cross-test both move a policy to a model it was not trained on. Why does one fail and the other succeed?

In the first the models are thin-airfoil theory and the RANS surrogate, about 0.2 apart in lift with different targets, and the surrogate-trained agent ends at 0.144, near the uncontrolled 0.151. In the second the two models were fitted to the same data and agree within 0.05, and scores stay between 0.0095 and 0.0106. Transfer works to the extent that the models agree where the policy flies.

Two neural networks sit in the surrogate-in-the-loop environment. Which one learns during training, how did the other one get its weights, and why does no gradient ever reach it?

The policy networks (actor and critics) learn: their weights change after each batch of 256 transitions, driven by the reward. The surrogate got its 6,690 weights earlier by supervised regression on 378 RANS cases (MSE, Adam, early stopping) and is then frozen. During reinforcement learning it is only called inside step(), 5 numbers in and 2 out; the loss is built from rewards and critic values, and its gradient is taken with respect to the actor and critic weights alone. The environment, surrogate included, is never differentiated, exactly as a CFD solver would not be.

Name three ways to keep the agent from exploiting surrogate error, and what each one did or would do in the runs of this lesson.

Monitor the range of αeq in every evaluation (PPO stayed within 4.4° to 5.6°; unprotected SAC with wide gusts reached 19.9°). Add a domain penalty with limits taken from the training data (time outside fell from 4.6 % to 0.8 %). Use an ensemble and watch its spread, which doubled outside the training angles. A fourth is the final check on a model not used in training.

Into Lesson 7

This lesson controlled two numbers of one airfoil with one flap, and it could afford a cheap model because lift and drag compress well. Turbulence does not offer that shortcut. In Lesson 7 the environment is a direct numerical simulation of a turbulent channel, the quantity to reduce is the wall friction, and the actuators are blowing and suction at every wall grid point: 256 agents in the minimal channel and 4,096 in the larger one. How do you train thousands of agents when every step is expensive again?

DRL for turbulence and flow control

The loop from Lesson 1 is now wrapped around a direct numerical simulation of turbulence. After this lesson you can explain how it scales to a whole wall through many identical agents, how a study is judged, and how the reward decides which physics the agent attacks.

From Lesson 6

Lesson 6 controlled one flap on one airfoil, and it trained on cheap models because CFD inside the loop was too expensive. The research in this lesson takes the opposite step: the environment is the expensive simulation, a direct numerical simulation (DNS) of a turbulent channel, and the thing being controlled is the turbulence itself. The question for this lesson: how can trial and error work when the wall has hundreds of actuators and every step costs a DNS time step?

The same loop, now with a DNS inside

Lesson 1: mass on a lineThis lesson: turbulent channel
Environmenttwo lines of PythonDNS of an open channel at friction Reynolds number Reτ = 180
Stateposition error and velocitystreamwise and wall-normal velocity fluctuations u′, v′ at y⁺ = 15
Actionone force in [−1, 1]a wall-normal velocity at every wall grid point, in [−uτ, uτ]
Rewardminus (miss distance + effort)relative reduction of the wall shear stress
rt = 1 − τw / τw,unc = RD    (averaged over the whole wall and over the time between two actions)

τw is the wall shear stress and "unc" means the uncontrolled flow, so the reward is the drag reduction RD itself. Every study in this lesson is model-free: the agent never sees the Navier–Stokes equations, only samples of interaction. The Markov decision process behind this is Lesson 2; the algorithms named below (DDPG, TD3, PPO) are Lesson 5.

The environment: a turbulent open channel

An open channel has a no-slip wall at the bottom and a symmetry condition at the top. That simplifies the outer layer and isolates the near-wall turbulence that produces the friction. The wall is the only place the agent can touch the flow, and one plane is the only place it can look.

A minimal channel is the smallest periodic box that still sustains near-wall turbulence. It is cheap and it holds a single low-speed streak, so the dynamics are simpler than in a real wall flow. The larger channel has several streaks that interact, which is physics the small box cannot show.

The yardstick: opposition control

vwall(x, z, t) = −α · [ v(x, ys, z, t) − ⟨v(x, ys, z, t)⟩ ]

ys is the height of the sensing plane, α a positive gain (usually 1), and ⟨·⟩ the mean over the plane. Subtracting the mean keeps the net mass flux through the wall at zero. It is a linear, proportional law. With sensing at y⁺ = 15 the implementation in the paper gave 25.67 % drag reduction, against about 25 % in the literature, which confirms the baseline was reproduced properly.

Key idea

This is Lesson 3's rule again: a learned controller means nothing without a classical reference next to it. On the point mass the references were PD and LQR. Here it is opposition control, and the environment was deliberately built from the same sensors and actuators so that the comparison is fair.

One agent for the whole wall does not scale. Many identical agents do.

Try the two set-ups on the wall of the minimal channel. Hover or click a tile to see what that cell observes and does.

With one agent, the action has as many components as there are actuators. Trial and error has to search a 256-dimensional action space, and the search grows beyond what exploration can cover: the curse of dimensionality. The way out comes from the flow itself. The channel is homogeneous and periodic along the wall, so its statistics are the same everywhere.

So the wall is cut into small regions called pseudo-environments. They are instantaneously different and statistically identical: different trajectories of the same problem. Each one is an agent with its own local state and its own action, and all of them share one network. That is multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) with a translationally invariant policy.

Training in parallelEvery tile contributes a transition at every solver step, from one simulation. With a wall cut into only 4 × 4 regions that already means 16 times the experience.
Small search spaceThe network's action stays one number, however many actuators the wall has.
Portable policyA local policy can be applied to a larger wall with more tiles, provided the physics it exploits is present there.
r(j) = λloc · r(j)loc + (1 − λloc) · rglob

The reward of agent j mixes a local part, computed in its own pseudo-environment, with a global part computed over the whole domain. A common reward is what makes the agents cooperate: each tile is paid for the drag of the whole wall, so no tile gains by improving its own patch at its neighbours' expense.

Rule of thumb

One agent could handle the regions one after another, but that is much less effective. With separate models and rewards each region optimises locally. With shared parameters and a collective reward the regions work together. Multi-agent training is the key to making reinforcement learning work in turbulence and other high-dimensional systems.

How the Fortran solver and the Python learner talk

The practical obstacle is two languages. The pseudo-spectral solver SIMSON is Fortran, parallelised with the Message Passing Interface (MPI). The reinforcement-learning libraries (for example Stable-Baselines3 and Tianshou, built for the Gymnasium interface of Lesson 5) are Python. The trick is MPI dynamic process management: Python spawns the solver, and an MPI intercommunicator carries states, reward and actions between the two groups.

The gain is that the validated parallel solver needs only minimal changes. The price is that dynamic process spawning does not work directly on every supercomputer. In Lesson 5 terms, process 0 is where step() lives: it takes the actions, lets the solver advance, and returns observations and reward.

Inside the agent: the actor, the critic and one update

What the agent achieved, and how it differs from the baseline

Two honest details from the paper. Learning was sensitive to the initial condition of the episodes, and not every training run produced a drag-reducing policy. The policies that did learn then performed consistently in testing from six different initial conditions. Neither controller relaminarised the flow, which at this Reynolds number would give the upper bound of 73.9 %.

The learned strategy is a two-step, bang-bang control: it switches between +uτ and −uτ and disrupts the near-wall cycle. Opposition control is linear by construction. The agent found a nonlinear strategy that no proportional law can express, and in the minimal channel it attenuates the streak through a streamwise travelling wave.

Quadrant analysis: what "no predominance of Q2 and Q4" means

Split every instant at the sensing plane by the signs of u′ and v′. Q2, an ejection: slow fluid (u′ < 0) moving away from the wall (v′ > 0). Q4, a sweep: fast fluid (u′ > 0) moving toward the wall (v′ < 0). In both, u′v′ is negative, and those are the events that carry the Reynolds shear stress and feed the wall friction. Ordinary wall turbulence is dominated by them.

Opposition control reduces the range of the fluctuations, yet ejections and sweeps still dominate. Under DRL the streamwise fluctuations drop, the wall-normal ones grow, and the four quadrants become evenly populated. "Lack of predominance of Q2 and Q4" therefore says the agent broke the mechanism that produces friction, where the baseline only turned its volume down. In the larger channel the same change appears, less evenly.

Does the saving survive the cost of actuation?

Blowing and suction need power. A controller that saves drag by spending more than it saves is useless, so the bookkeeping has two lines.

Win = ½ |vwall|³     Snet = [ cf,unc − (cf + Win) ] / cf,unc = RD − Win / cf,unc

Snet is the net energy saving, cf the skin-friction coefficient, and Win the actuation power per unit wall area (after Kametani et al.). The second form reads: net saving = drag reduction minus actuation power as a fraction of the uncontrolled friction. The later study counted the power more strictly, adding the pressure work at the wall and allowing no energy recovery. Then the cost is of order 10⁻⁴ and it separates the controllers.

Pitfall

Report both numbers. The actuation cost is recovered as RD − Snet, and it can reorder controllers: the bang-bang policy trained on the drag reward pays 6.0 points for its 31.9, twice what the SHAP policy pays. Also watch the units. "5.6 % better" (a ratio of two drag reductions) and "1.8 points better" (their difference) describe the same pair of results.

The reward decides which physics the agent attacks

Lesson 1 said the reward is the only channel through which the goal reaches the agent. This study tests that statement on turbulence. The wall shear stress is the symptom; the structures that keep the near-wall cycle alive are the disease. Earlier work used SHAP (Shapley additive explanations) to rank how much each flow region matters for predicting the future flow, and found that the important regions overlap only partly with the classical structures.

So three rewards replace the drag by a volume integral: Q events (with U the long-time mean profile), streaks, and the magnitude of the SHAP field. Computing SHAP values inside a training loop would be far too slow, so a U-Net trained on uncontrolled flow predicts the SHAP field from the velocity, over 200 times faster. The policies were trained in the minimal channel and evaluated in the larger one over 150 initial conditions.

The SHAP policy gives 33.7 % drag reduction and 30.6 % net saving, the best in both. The Q-event policy is the best at reducing Q events and streaks, yet worse at reducing drag, which says the classical structures are not the most important ones to target. The SHAP actuation is also more targeted: it rarely reaches the bounds and needs about half the power of the drag-reward policy.

Intuition

The shear stress is the symptom and the underlying structures are the disease. Going after the disease gave better performance, with fewer large oscillations and a much lower control power.

Why would a proxy beat the real objective? The authors' reading is partial observability. The agent sees one plane, so the problem is not fully Markovian (Lesson 2), and the SHAP field acts as a sophisticated form of reward shaping: a signal that points at the cause before the drag responds. Ordinary reward shaping is limited by the expert who designs the proxy. Here the proxy is identified from data by an explainable model.

Separation bubbles: learning the forcing a human would tune by hand

Here the agent does not pick a velocity at every wall point. It learns one number per step: the amplitude ay(t) of a prescribed Gaussian-shaped body force that emulates blowing and suction. The state is 24 streamwise-velocity probes upstream of and inside the bubble, and the reward is the time-averaged bubble length. The baseline is the classical one for separation: periodic (harmonic) forcing at a fixed frequency.

The rule to draw from this case: train on the cheapest simulation that still captures the main flow features, and deploy on the expensive one. That is Lesson 6's idea carried to a turbulent flow, with a coarse grid playing the role the surrogate played for the airfoil.

Rayleigh–Bénard convection: single agent against multi-agent, same problem

A fluid between a hot bottom wall and a cold top wall forms convection cells that carry heat upward. The goal is less heat transfer. This case matters for the guide because it runs the two set-ups of the wall-grid figure above on the same problem with the same training budget.

After 350 episodes the multi-agent policy had cut Nu by 22.7 %, the single agent by about 5.1 %. Two reasons follow from the picture. The multi-agent network solves a one-output problem instead of a ten-output one, and it receives ten times the experience from each simulation: 2,000 actions against 200.

What the agents found, on their own: concentrating heat near the centre breaks the second convection cell and establishes one larger cell with a lower heat-transfer rate. That state is stable and persists when the control is switched off. The cooperation comes from the common reward; there is no message passing between neighbours.

Cylinder wakes: the strategy changes when the physics changes

In two dimensions (Varela et al., 2022) the agent rediscovers an opposition-type strategy up to Re = 1000 and switches to a different mechanism at Re = 2000, where the drag coefficient falls from 3.39 to 2.79, over 17 %. The shedding is weakened, not suppressed. The controlled flow looks more like that around an airfoil, with separation delayed and the Strouhal number shifted toward lower frequencies.

In practice

The same line of work is being taken to the laboratory: a cylinder with a fully turbulent wake and loudspeakers as actuators. A cylinder is chosen because it produces a lot of drag, so an effect is easy to measure. SHAP is used to identify the particular eddies responsible for the drag, and DRL trains the speakers to find the frequencies that damp exactly those. The claim to take from it is a measured one: classical control is not useless, and an expert in it might build a fine controller, but DRL gets there faster, and in a nonlinear way.

Five questions to ask of any flow-control study

On transfer: from the minimal to the full channel everything was done without retraining, and for a moderate rise in Reynolds number zero-shot transfer is good too, though some retraining can help. On cost: a DNS in the loop is less prohibitive than it sounds, because training can be accelerated and a decently resolved large-eddy simulation is accurate enough; a very poor simulation loses features that matter.

Pitfall

Partial observation is the quiet assumption in all of these. One plane of velocity or a ring of pressure probes does not determine the next state of a turbulent flow, so the Markov property of Lesson 2 holds only approximately. Controlling the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation of Lesson 5 from only a few sensors is the small-scale version of exactly this.

Common questions, takeaways, and the papers

The answers below summarise what the studies listed at the end of this section report, and how their authors discuss the limits of their results.

What data must be provided to train the agent?

None. It is given an environment, a simulation or an experiment, and finds its policy by interacting with it. Knowledge of the problem enters through the design instead, for example the invariance that multi-agent RL exploits.

Do the agents communicate with their neighbours, and do they end up with different policies?

The policy is the same, because the model is the same and is trained in parallel for all agents. Each agent acts differently because its observation is different. What they share is the reward, and the common reward is what makes them cooperate.

Is a DNS inside a training loop too expensive, and does lower resolution lose scales that matter?

Training can be accelerated considerably and reduced resolution works: training with large-eddy simulation has been very accurate. A very poor simulation loses features, so there is a trade-off. The same approach is being used in wind-tunnel experiments.

Can a simple control law be extracted from the trained network?

In general no. The policy is a high-dimensional nonlinear mapping. The network is fast to evaluate, in milliseconds, and such policies are being deployed in real time in wind-tunnel experiments.

Does a policy trained in the minimal channel transfer?

All transfers from the minimal to the larger channel were done without retraining. For a moderate increase in Reynolds number zero-shot transfer is also good; sometimes some retraining helps.

In the 2D cylinder, is shedding suppressed? What happens to the Strouhal number?

Shedding is weakened, not removed. Separation is delayed, the flow looks more like that around an airfoil, and the Strouhal number moves toward lower frequencies.

How does this compare with control built on a reduced model such as POD?

A proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) model simplifies the dynamics significantly, so in principle it gives less effective control. The DRL agent interacts with the full dynamics in the environment. (Sensor noise from experiments does affect the policy, which is why high-fidelity measurements are needed.)

Key takeaways

  • For flows with homogeneous directions, use multi-agent RL with a shared, translationally invariant policy and a collective reward. Single-agent RL scales poorly.
  • In the channel at Reτ = 180, DRL reached 43 % (minimal) and 30 % (larger) drag reduction against 26 % and 20 % for linear opposition control, with a bang-bang actuation that evens out the quadrants.
  • Net energy saving is drag reduction minus actuation power relative to the uncontrolled friction. Report both, since the cost can reorder controllers.
  • Reward the cause, not the symptom: the SHAP-based reward beat the drag reward in drag (33.7 % against 31.9 %) with half the power.
  • Train on the cheapest environment that keeps the main physics (coarse grid, large-eddy simulation, minimal channel, lower Reynolds number) and deploy zero-shot, retraining only for large changes.

Several of the flow-control studies in this lesson were published together with their code and reinforcement-learning set-up, so those cases can be reproduced and modified.

Connect the dots: this lesson

The single loop scaled to turbulence without changing shape. What changed is how many copies of the agent run at once, how expensive one turn of the loop is, and how carefully the reward and the evaluation have to be designed. Every family of results above is the same recipe: a solver as environment, local agents on a homogeneous direction, a classical baseline, and a transfer test.

The whole guide on one page

  1. The learning loop. An agent acts, the environment answers with a state and a reward, and the reward is the only channel through which the goal reaches the agent.
  2. Values and Bellman. The value of a state is its reward plus the discounted value of its successors; Q is the form that yields a policy without a model.
  3. REINFORCE. Weight the log-probability of each action by the return that followed it, and always put a classical controller (PD, LQR) next to the result.
  4. Actor–critic on PDEs. A critic turns noisy returns into advantages; the solver is the environment; ask for reachable targets and see where LQR still wins.
  5. Algorithm families and Gymnasium. On-policy PPO is stable and wasteful with data, off-policy DDPG and TD3 reuse data; the reset/step interface lets library algorithms drive any solver.
  6. Airfoil and surrogates. When the simulator is too expensive, train on a cheaper model of it, and check fidelity and extrapolation before trusting the controller.
  7. Turbulence and multi-agent RL. Homogeneous directions let many local agents share one policy; judge by baseline, transfer and net energy; the reward decides which physics is attacked.

Things to try next

  • Kuramoto–Sivashinsky in Gymnasium (Lesson 5): fewer actuators, fewer sensors, a different domain length. These are the one-dimensional versions of this lesson's actuation, partial-observation and transfer questions. Train once, then change one of the three and test without retraining.
  • The same experiment with a different goal (keep the energy below a threshold instead of driving it to zero): a small experiment in "the reward decides the physics", including its effect on control effort.
  • The surrogate-in-the-loop airfoil experiment (Lesson 6). Compare PPO, SAC and TD3 at equal numbers of interactions, test the sensitivity to Reynolds number, vary the reward weights, and train with a randomised Reynolds number: the airfoil-scale versions of the algorithm, transfer and reward questions above.
  • The airfoil experiment with the 0-D model (Lesson 6). Hide the gust from the agent, and change the smoothness penalty: partial observation and actuation cost on a model that trains in minutes.
  • The heat, Burgers and Kuramoto–Sivashinsky experiments (Lesson 4). Restrict the sensors, change the physical parameters, and add a nonlinear model-predictive controller as a baseline. Good practice in the baseline rule.
  • A latent-space experiment: build latent spaces of the AirfRANS fields with 10, 20 and 30 dimensions and measure the energy captured. It runs on an ordinary computer and prepares the reduced-model route of Lesson 6.
  • The open codes of the papers above. Start with the review by Vignon, Rabault and Vinuesa, then the channel code of Guastoni et al.

Check yourself

Why is the channel problem handled with 256 agents instead of one, and what property of the flow permits it?

One agent would have to choose 256 wall velocities at once, a search space that trial and error cannot cover. The channel is homogeneous and periodic along the wall, so every wall cell faces statistically the same problem. One small network, shared by all cells, then learns from 256 transitions per solver step and has a one-number action.

The policy trained in the minimal channel gives 43 % there and 30 % in the larger channel. Is that a failure of generalisation?

No. It ran without retraining and still beat opposition control, 30 % against 20 %. The drop is attributed to physics the minimal channel cannot contain, such as the interaction of several streaks. It does show why the transfer test has to be run and reported.

A controller reports 31.9 % drag reduction and 25.9 % net energy saving. What does it spend on actuation, and why does that matter for a ranking?

It spends 31.9 − 25.9 = 6.0 points of the uncontrolled friction. The Q-event policy reduces drag less (26.9 %) but spends only 0.5 points, so its net saving, 26.4 %, is higher. Ranking by drag reduction alone would put them in the wrong order.

What does "lack of predominance of Q2 and Q4 events" tell you about the DRL-controlled flow?

In uncontrolled wall turbulence ejections (Q2) and sweeps (Q4) dominate the joint distribution of u′ and v′; they carry the Reynolds shear stress. Opposition control shrinks the distribution and keeps that dominance. Under DRL the four quadrants are evenly populated, so the mechanism itself was changed.

Across the guide: the point-mass reward of Lesson 1 had an effort term, the first channel reward did not. What does the effort term do, and what replaced it here?

On the point mass the term 0.01·F² charged for force inside the reward, so the agent learned to stop pushing. The first channel study rewarded drag reduction only and the policy became bang-bang; its cost was checked afterwards through the net energy saving. The SHAP-reward study shows the other route: a better-aimed reward produced a gentler actuation with half the power.

In the multi-agent anatomy loop, which components exist once and which exist 256 times?

The actor's forward pass and its exploration noise run 256 times per step, once per cell, but with one set of weights θ. The replay buffer, the critic, the update rule and the reward exist once: the 256 transitions of a step are pooled into the one buffer, the one reward is paid to every copy, and the one new θ is the policy of every copy. Remove the sharing and the same drawing shows one agent with 512 inputs and 256 outputs.

In one DDPG update of the channel agent, where does the gradient of the loss go, and where does it never go?

The loss (y − Q(s, a))² is computed from stored transitions, so its gradient reaches the critic weights ω, and through the slope ∂Q/∂a it reaches the actor weights θ. It never passes through the DNS: the solver is called to produce s′ and r, and the U-Net inside the SHAP reward is frozen, so neither is differentiated.

Across the guide: Lesson 6 trained on a surrogate because CFD in the loop was too expensive. Name three ways the studies in this lesson made a real solver affordable inside the loop.

Multi-agent training multiplies the experience from each solver step (256 transitions per step in the minimal channel). Off-policy algorithms with a replay buffer reuse every DNS transition (Lesson 5). And training happens on the cheapest case that keeps the physics, a minimal channel, a coarse grid or a lower Reynolds number, with deployment on the expensive case without retraining.

End of the guide

You started with a mass on a line and one arrow going round a loop. You can now read a current flow-control paper and ask the right things of it: what is the state, the action and the reward; how many agents and why; which algorithm and why that one; what is the baseline; does it transfer; what does the actuation cost. The loop never changed. Go back to the experiments of the earlier lessons, change one thing at a time, and predict the outcome before you run it.
